title: Predicting War: The Science of Geopolitical Forecasting
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: What if you could foresee the next major conflict months before the first shot is fired? Geopolitical forecasting blends game theory, expert analysis, and AI to predict wars, economic fallout, and humanitarian crises. From Cold War-era scenario planning at RAND to modern machine learning models crunching satellite data, this episode dives into the methods—and limitations—of anticipating global conflict. We examine historical failures (like the Yom Kippur War intelligence breakdown) and cutting-edge tools like DARPA's Snow Globe, where AI personas simulate crises. The stakes couldn't be higher: in a world of black swan events, forecasting isn't just academic—it's a survival tool. Show Notes ### The Art and Science of Predicting Conflict Geopolitical forecasting aims to reduce uncertainty in an inherently chaotic system: international conflict. Unlike weather or economic predictions, it must account for human agency—leaders' decisions, institutional friction, and shifting public morale. The field's roots trace back to Cold War game theory, where models like mutually assured destruction framed nuclear strategy. RAND Corporation later pioneered scenario planning, stress-testing multiple futures to avoid surprise. #### Traditional Tools and Their Blind Spots Early methods included expert panels (like the CIA's "Red Cell") and game theory applications, such as modeling arms races via prisoner's dilemmas. Yet these approaches struggled with biases—analysts often fit data to preexisting narratives. Static models also faltered against black swan events, exemplified by the 1973 Yom Kippur War. Israel and the U.S. dismissed warning signs because their framework assumed Egypt and Syria wouldn't attack if victory seemed impossible. #### The AI Revolution Modern machine learning processes vast datasets—news archives, satellite imagery, financial transactions—to flag instability. Some models achieve 80–95% accuracy by detecting nonlinear patterns, like correlating state-media rhetoric with oligarch banking activity. But "black box" predictions lack explainability, a hurdle for policymakers. Projects like DARPA's Snow Globe address this by simulating crises with AI personas (e.g., a U.S. Secretary of Defense or Chinese Politburo member), generating plausible decision chains rather than raw probabilities. #### The Forecast Feedback Loop Forecasts don't just predict; they influence outcomes. Historical examples like Halford Mackinder's "Heartland Theory" (which shaped Nazi and Cold War strategies) show how predictions become geopolitical actors. Today, divergent forecasts—such as U.S. and Israeli assessments of the Iran nuclear deal—highlight how assumptions drive policy. The challenge remains: balancing precision with adaptability in a world where the next crisis might defy all models. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/geopolitical-forecasting-war-prediction

title: Prediction of groundwater nitrogen metabolic potential based on fluorescence information: An integrated semi-supervised learning-automated machine learning approach
authors: Zongyi Peng; 郭建阳; You Mou; Yezhi Yang; Yi Li; Longfei Wang
abstract: Nitrogen pollution is a major environmental challenge in groundwater systems, and identifying nitrogen metabolic potential is essential for understanding its development and transformation. However, functional characterization relies on metagenomic data, while conventional water-quality monitoring does not directly quantify pathway-specific N-cycle gene abundance. Fluorescence spectroscopy offers a rapid and convenient alternative, but its predictive potential for groundwater nitrogen metabolism remains insufficiently explored. In this study, 3D-EEM fluorescence spectroscopy was integrated with the H2O automated machine learning (AutoML) framework and five reference machine-learning algorithms to predict seven N-cycle gene-abundance targets. Two datasets were used: an original dataset comprising 91 measured samples and an SSL-expanded dataset constructed by screening a candidate pool of 152 records from previous studies through semi-supervised learning (SSL). By generating pseudo-labels based on spectral-functional relationships learned from the measured samples, SSL expanded the training set and enhanced the model’s ability to capture nonlinear relationships. The SSL-H2O AutoML model provided pathway-dependent improvements, with R 2 values of 0.940 and 0.885 for denitrification and nitrogen fixation, respectively. Following SSL-based dataset expansion, the normalized importance of C2 doubled from 16.2% to 32.4%, indicating that SSL strengthened the model’s recognition of this key predictor. These results demonstrate the advantage of SSL under limited labeled data and highlight the potential of machine learning for predicting groundwater nitrogen metabolic potential. This framework provides a rapid and cost-effective supplement to metagenomic characterization and supports applications of data-driven approaches in groundwater research.

title: PREreview of "Beyond Static Sandboxing: Learned Capability Governance for Autonomous AI Agents"
authors: Karmendra Pandey
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23197319. ## Summary This paper names a problem every agent deployer has felt but few have measured: open-source agent runtimes like OpenClaw expose every tool to every session by default — a summarization task gets shell execution, subagent spawning, and credential access, a 15x over-provision the authors call the capability overprovisioning problem. They propose AgentWarden (titled "Aethelgard" in the abstract), a governance middleware with three parts: a Capability Governor that scopes which tools the agent is even told about per session (via AGENTS.md injection plus a deny list), a Safety Router that intercepts every tool call before execution using a hybrid rule-based plus fine-tuned LLM classifier, and a PPO policy trained on the audit log to learn the minimum viable tool set per task type. The Skill Economy Ratio (SER) — fraction of exposed tools actually invoked — formalizes least privilege as a measurable property. On a live OpenClaw deployment, the system blocks 26.2% of 447 intercepted tool calls (exec and sessions_spawn blocked at 100%) and neutralizes 92% of 100 adversarial tasks. On AgentDojo (97 tasks, 949 injection cases) it holds benign utility at 89.7% (−1.0pp) while reducing attack success rate by only 1.4pp overall. The paper documents a genuinely interesting finding: prompt injection that succeeds at the LLM level can still fail at the infrastructure level. The limitations section is unusually candid about PPO collapse, classifier data scarcity, and what the system does not cover. ## Strengths 1. The core insight is correct and underappreciated. "An agent cannot misuse a tool it does not know exists" — scoping capability awareness, not just execution permission, is the right layer for least privilege, and SER gives the field a metric to argue about instead of vibes. 2. Honest about the threat-surface boundary. The paper clearly states that the router governs tool calls while important_instructions-style attacks operate at the LLM reasoning boundary — and the AgentDojo results demonstrate it. This kind of scoped honesty is exactly what practitioners need to place a defense correctly. 3. The infrastructure-vs-model finding is valuable. Showing that qwen2.5:7b generates dangerous calls the infrastructure catches, while DeepSeek-chat refuses at the model level, makes the defense-in-depth thesis concrete rather than slogan-level. 4. Multi-runtime validation. Testing the middleware across OpenClaw, DeepAgents, and Hermes wire formats (including XML tool calls) shows this is built as infrastructure, not a demo. ## Major comments 1. The PPO policy collapsed in production testing. Both PPO checkpoints degenerated to single-tool policies (predicting only memory_search for all task types) — a known artifact of SER-maximizing training in synthetic environments. The paper is honest about this, but it means the headline "learned policy" does not actually work outside simulation; the YAML fallback did the real work. The learned-governance claim should be downgraded until the policy is retrained on real session data, as the authors themselves plan. 2. The AgentDojo results undercut the headline numbers. On the independent benchmark, ASR moves from 90.3% to 88.9% — a 1.4pp reduction. The 100% block rates come from the authors' own 100 hand-crafted adversarial tasks. Both are reported, which I respect, but the abstract leans on the friendlier numbers. 3. The classifier is not production-ready by the authors' own account. The fine-tuned router trained on 273 examples with a 95/5 class imbalance, and the base Qwen2.5-1.5B "performs poorly" without fine-tuning. A production-quality classifier needs 2,000–5,000 balanced examples (their estimate). The ~800ms–2s LLM-stage latency per tool call also compounds in long agent loops — a per-task latency analysis is missing. 4. Name and structure inconsistencies. The abstract calls the system "Aethelgard" and "four layer"; the body says "AgentWarden" and "three-layer." For a security paper, where precision is the product, this sloppiness undermines confidence. 5. The router inspects tool calls, not reasoning text. The paper documents a reverse-shell case where the model returned instructions as text with no tool call and the router saw nothing. This is a fundamental architectural boundary, correctly identified — but it means the system's protection assumes the dangerous action goes through a tool call, which a clever agent or prompt injection need not do. ## Minor comments 1. The evaluation dataset is "available upon request" rather than public — for a security paper making empirical claims, public release (sanitized) would materially strengthen trust. 2. The DeepAgents LocalShellBackend bypass finding is important and well documented; it deserves a line in the abstract's scope statement. ## Overall assessment Recommend with major revisions. The capability-scoping framing, SER metric, and infrastructure-level enforcement are sound contributions that the field needs. But the collapsed RL policy, the thin classifier training data, and the gap between hand-crafted adversarial results and AgentDojo performance mean the "learned" and "adaptive" claims currently outrun the evidence. Fix the naming inconsistencies, fence the claims to what the production tests actually show, and this becomes a paper I would cite when designing agent deployments. title: Published October 22, 2026 | Version v1 Other Open RADIX and the Integrated Information Architecture: Structural Addressing, Multiscale Fingerprints, Conditional Authority, and Evidence-Gated Validation PART III
authors: Egidijus Kasiulevičius; Azuolas Kasiulevicius; Saule Kasiuleviciute; Ausra Kasiuleviciene
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: RADIX × SPARC: Topological Addressing, Identity Preservation, and Evidence-Gated Integration A research report on structural information addressing and the RADIX–EGIDA–LASO-Σ–KASK-Q–BITE CORE–AUŠRA architecture Authors: Ąžuolas Kasiulevičius, Saulė Kasiulevičiūtė, Egidijus Kasiulevičius, Aušra Kasiulevičienė Version: Research manuscript draft v0.1Date: 23 October 2026Intended repository: ZenodoStatus: Preliminary research report; independent reproduction and full production integration remain pending. Abstract This paper presents the RADIX approach to structural and topological information addressing and reports its preliminary evaluation using the SPARC galaxy rotation-curve dataset. The central design principle is that an address, an identity, and an authorization decision are different entities. A structural address can guide retrieval, but it must not independently establish the identity of a record or authorize an operation. The proposed architecture separates structural representation, candidate retrieval, exact record verification, conditional authorization, transition analysis, and coordinated action. RADIX supplies the structural addressing layer; EGIDA is responsible for object retrieval; LASO-Σ retains authority over whether an operation may proceed; and KASK-Q, BITE CORE, and AUŠRA are intended to provide complementary transition analysis, integrity controls, and adaptive control functions. Previously reported experiments used the public SPARC dataset, which contains observations and mass-model information for 175 disk galaxies. The project reports 3,391 numeric records in its processed representation, 1,643 occupied address buckets, and 531 collision groups containing differing feature vectors. These results demonstrate why an address cannot safely be treated as a unique identity. A more recent reported identity-gate test achieved 10/10 PASS on its defined test contract, while the complete production integration remains blocked. Preliminary predictive experiments do not establish universal superiority over conventional methods: RADIX-16 achieved a weighted mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.190254, compared with 0.193220 for AR(2) and 0.181191 for Spline-8 on one reported fixed evaluation. The results therefore support further investigation of identity-preserving structural addressing, not a claim of a new astrophysical discovery. The paper defines the proposed contribution, summarizes reported evidence, identifies unresolved limitations, and specifies the requirements for independent reproduction. Keywords: topological addressing; structural information retrieval; record identity; collision handling; data integrity; RADIX; EGIDA; SPARC; evidence-gated authorization; reproducible research. 1. Introduction Information systems commonly use keys, indexes, hashes, graph relationships, and similarity measures to locate records. These mechanisms solve related but different problems. A search key helps locate candidates; a record identity establishes which object is being referenced; and an authorization mechanism determines whether an action is permitted. The RADIX research program investigates whether information can be addressed through its position and relationships within a structured representation rather than relying exclusively on conventional flat indexing or similarity search. The intended model is topological in the broad computational sense: the address is derived from a structured representation of information and its relationships. The project also explores how such addressing can operate within a larger architecture without replacing the authority rules of the receiving systems. This research uses SPARC as a real-data stress environment. SPARC is a public collection of rotation curves and related mass-model data for 175 disk galaxies. It was introduced by Lelli, McGaugh, and Schombert (2016). The purpose of this paper is not to claim that topological retrieval, hashing, or graph-based search are new in themselves. Existing work already investigates topology-aware retrieval. The narrower research question is whether a specific combination of structural addressing, collision preservation, exact identity verification, and separately enforced authorization can be implemented and tested as a coherent architecture. 1.1 Research questions This work addresses four questions: Can a deterministic structural address be used to retrieve candidate records reproducibly? Can collisions and duplicate records be preserved without silently confusing candidate location with record identity? Can retrieval be integrated with authorization controls while leaving the original authority logic unchanged? Do preliminary SPARC prediction experiments provide evidence that the addressing framework improves scientific prediction, or is its demonstrated contribution currently limited to data organization and identity handling? 2. Proposed contribution and design principles The principal design rule is: Address ≠ Identity ≠ Authority. These three concepts must remain separate throughout the system. Address: a structural key used to locate one or more candidate records. Identity: evidence establishing which record is intended, including exact source information and any required record identifier. Authority: the existing policy and decision logic governing whether an action is permitted. The proposed contribution is a modular architecture that enforces these distinctions across retrieval and downstream action. 2.1 Structural addressing RADIX represents information through an address derived from a defined structural encoding. The address is intended to make the organization and retrieval of information explicit and reproducible. The exact encoding, normalization rules, feature ordering, precision, node registry, and version must be fixed for a reproducible implementation. A structural address should not be interpreted as a proof of uniqueness unless uniqueness has been demonstrated under the relevant data model. 2.2 Identity-preserving retrieval The retrieval process must preserve all records that map to the same address. It must then apply the required identity checks rather than automatically accepting the first candidate. A conceptual retrieval sequence is: Construct the address using a fixed version of the addressing rules. Retrieve every candidate associated with that address. verify source identifiers and exact or otherwise formally specified identity evidence. Preserve legitimate duplicates and collisions. Reject or quarantine ambiguous cases when the required identity cannot be established. This procedure makes correctness the primary requirement and treats retrieval speed as a secondary optimization. 2.3 Evidence-gated authorization A successful lookup is not an authorization decision. RADIX must not override the original LASO-Σ authority logic, thresholds, or policy rules. EGIDA may identify the intended object, but the receiving system must independently decide whether the requested action is allowed. The intended architecture is therefore a sequence of separable responsibilities: Structural representation → RADIX addressing → EGIDA retrieval and identity checks → existing authorization rules → downstream control or action. KASK-Q, BITE CORE, and AUŠRA are intended to provide additional analysis and control functions. Their full integration must be demonstrated using the original implementations and interfaces before the complete architecture can be declared validated. 3. Data and provenance 3.1 SPARC source The primary scientific stress dataset is: Lelli, F., McGaugh, S. S., & Schombert, J. M. (2016). SPARC: Mass Models for 175 Disk Galaxies with Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curves. The Astronomical Journal, 152, 157. https://doi.org/10.3847/0004-6256/152/6/157 Dataset record: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16284118 The project used the SPARC rotation-curve archive Rotmod_LTG.zip. The source record lists the archive's MD5 checksum as e4c8b92766026770ed35e5889064e12b. A separate project manifest has reported a SHA-256 value of 0a80cc90714828cc28b7dd57923576714d209f2490328c087c4a4ad607faf588. These checksum values are provenance references from the project's earlier records; they must be recalculated against the exact input bytes used in the final reproducibility package. A checksum establishes byte-level correspondence to a known file, not scientific correctness or authenticity by itself. 3.2 Processed records The project's previously reported processed representation contains: 175 galaxy files. 3,916 physical source-line records in the earlier source audit. 3,391 numeric records used in the reported address-bucket analysis. These counts refer to different stages of processing and must not be treated as interchangeable. The final package should include the exact parsing rules, excluded-line accounting, record manifest, and code required to reproduce each count. 4. Methods 4.1 Address construction and collision analysis The project constructed deterministic addresses for the processed numeric records and grouped records sharing an address. The reported analysis distinguishes the number of records from the number of occupied address buckets and from the number of collision groups. A collision group is not necessarily a data error. Different records may legitimately share a coarse or rounded structural address. The critical correctness requirement is that a collision must not silently erase a record or cause the system to select an incorrect identity. For that reason, the audit evaluates candidate preservation and exact identity verification separately from address generation. 4.2 Correctness audit The project's RADIX correctness-audit framework includes the following categories: C1: deterministic repeatability. title: RateSniffer: A Lightweight and Robust Website Fingerprinting Defense via Rate-Aware Morphing
authors: Zi-Yi Zhou; Xian-Wen Deng; Weiqi Bai; Yi-Jun Wang; Zhi Xue
venue: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abstract: Website Fingerprinting (WF) attacks pose a serious threat to user privacy in anonymity networks, such as Tor, as attackers can infer visited websites by analyzing encrypted traffic patterns. Existing WF defenses suffer from a persistent trade-off between robustness and efficiency. To address this challenge, we propose RateSniffer, a lightweight and robust WF defense that leverages rate-aware adaptive morphing to efficiently obfuscate traffic patterns. RateSniffer comprises two key components: Rate-Aware Feature Region Extraction, which employs Grad-CAM to identify traffic regions most influential to WF classifiers and construct rate-aware templates; and Rate-Aware Adaptive Morphing, which selectively perturbs live Tor traffic by matching short-term sending rates to these templates. Extensive experiments on a real-world Tor dataset against six representative WF attacks and six state-of-the-art defenses show that RateSniffer reduces the accuracies of different WF attacks down to 13.02%-55.73%, with only 47% bandwidth and 11% time overhead. Notably, RateSniffer further decreases attack accuracy by up to 15 percentage points compared to the strongest existing defense, significantly outperforming all prior methods.

title: Real or fake motion: protecting virtual reality (VR) behavioral authentication systems against motion forecasting attacks
authors: Mingjun Li; Natasha Kholgade Banerjee; Sean K. Banerjee
abstract: As virtual reality (VR) systems are used in serious applications, such as physical therapy for rehabilitation, workforce training in military scenarios, or in the classroom, protecting user data from malicious agents is critical in ensuring trust in the VR system. Over the past half decade approaches in behavioral biometrics have explored the use of user motion as a mechanism for authentication and identification in VR. Approaches in using motion forecasting for behavioral biometrics in VR enable the use of limited user data by forecasting future behavior for user authentication. Such techniques enhance security by limiting the amount of user data exposed to a malicious agent. However, recent techniques have exposed an emergent vulnerability, wherein a malicious agent can use a motion forecasting model to generate plausible behavior of the target user to attack a virtual reality system protected using behavioral biometrics. In this paper, we present the first approach for classifying whether a user trajectory presented to a VR authentication system is an authentic or a deepfake trajectory. In this case, an authentic, or real, trajectory would be the motion data generated from the VR device through the actions of the intended user. On the other hand, a deepfake, or fake, trajectory would be motion synthetically generated using a deep learning-based motion forecasting approach that is used to masquerade as the motion of the intended user. Our approach uses a fully convolutional network (FCN) to determine whether a trajectory is real or fake. Using the 3D position data for the right-hand controller from the 41-subject Miller et al. ball throwing dataset collected using 3 VR systems, namely a Meta Quest, HTC Vive, and HTC Vive Cosmos, we show that our approach achieves accuracies up to 0.997, 0.998, and 0.992 when discriminating real and fake trajectories. Our approach provides the first protection against motion forecasting-based attacks against VR authentication systems. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Terascale-All-sensing-Research-Studio/Real_or_Fake_VR_Motion .

title: ReMIA: a Powerful and Efficient Alternative to Membership Inference Attacks against Synthetic Data Generators
authors: Davide Scassola; Andrea Coser; Sebastiano Saccani
abstract: Tabular data sharing under privacy constraints is increasingly important for research and collaboration. Synthetic data generators (SDGs) are a promising solution, but synthetic data remains vulnerable to attacks, such as membership inference attacks (MIAs), which aim to determine whether a specific record was part of the training data. State-of-the-art MIAs are powerful but impractical: they rely on shadow modeling, requiring hundreds of SDG training runs, and need auxiliary data several times larger than the original training set. Fast proxy metrics like distance to closest record (DCR) are efficient but have limited sensitivity to MIA risk. We introduce ReMIA (Relative Membership Inference Attack), a practical privacy metric that requires only two SDG training runs and additional data no larger than the original training set. Rather than predicting whether a record was in the training set, ReMIA generates two synthetic datasets from two source datasets and measures whether a classifier can identify which source a record came from. Experiments across multiple tabular datasets and SDGs show that ReMIA has a sensitivity comparable to state-of-the-art MIAs while being substantially more practical. We further observe that SDGs can achieve privacy-utility trade-offs that traditional noise-based anonymization methods do not match. Code is available at https://github.com/aindo-com/remia.

title: Rounding-Guided Backdoor Injection in Deep Learning Model Quantization
authors: Xiangxiang Chen; Peixin Zhang; Jun Sun; Wenhai Wang; Jingyi Wang
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
abstract: Model quantization is a popular technique for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained environments.However, it may also introduce previously overlooked security risks.In this work, we present QURA, a novel backdoor attack that exploits model quantization to embed malicious behaviors.Unlike conventional backdoor attacks relying on training data poisoning or model training manipulation, QURA solely works using the quantization operations.In particular, QURA first employs a novel weight selection strategy to identify critical weights that influence the backdoor target (with the goal of perserving the model's overall performance in mind).Then, by optimizing the rounding direction of these weights, we amplify the backdoor effect across model layers without degrading accuracy.Extensive experiments demonstrate that QURA achieves nearly 100% attack success rates in most cases, with negligible performance degradation.Furthermore, we show that QURA can adapt to bypass existing backdoor defenses, underscoring its threat potential.Our findings highlight critical vulnerability in widely used model quantization process, emphasizing the need for more robust security measures.Our implementation is available at https://github.com/cxx122/QuRA.

title: SafeRedir: Prompt Embedding Redirection for Robust Unlearning in Image Generation Models
authors: Renyang Liu; Kangjie Chen; Han Qiu; Jie Zhang; Kwok-Yan Lam; Tianwei Zhang et al.
abstract: Image generation models (IGMs), while capable of producing impressive and creative content, often memorize a wide range of undesirable concepts from their training data, leading to the reproduction of unsafe content such as NSFW imagery and copyrighted artistic styles. Such behaviors pose persistent safety and compliance risks in real-world deployments and cannot be reliably mitigated by post-hoc filtering, owing to the limited robustness of such mechanisms and a lack of fine-grained semantic control. Recent unlearning methods seek to erase harmful concepts at the model level, which exhibit the limitations of requiring costly retraining, degrading the quality of benign generations, or failing to withstand prompt paraphrasing and adversarial attacks. To address these challenges, we introduce SafeRedir, a lightweight inference-time framework for robust unlearning via prompt embedding redirection. Without modifying the underlying IGMs, SafeRedir adaptively routes unsafe prompts toward safe semantic regions through token-level interventions in the embedding space. The framework comprises two core components: a latent-aware multi-modal safety classifier for identifying unsafe generation trajectories, and a token-level delta generator for precise semantic redirection, equipped with auxiliary predictors for token masking and adaptive scaling to localize and regulate the intervention. Empirical results across multiple representative unlearning tasks demonstrate that SafeRedir achieves effective unlearning capability, high semantic and perceptual preservation, robust image quality, and enhanced resistance to adversarial attacks. Furthermore, SafeRedir generalizes effectively across a variety of diffusion backbones and existing unlearned models, validating its plug-and-play compatibility and broad applicability. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ryliu68/SafeRedir.

title: Scam Link Detector Using Machine Learning
authors: Dhanaji Jadhav; Prashant Bedage
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a machine learning based Scam Link Detector system developed to identify phishing and malicious URLs using URL analysis and cybersecurity techniques. The proposed system analyzes suspicious URL patterns such as domain length, special characters, HTTPS validation, and phishing keywords to classify URLs as safe or unsafe. The system is implemented using Python, Flask, HTML, CSS, and machine learning algorithms. The project helps improve cybersecurity awareness and protects users from online scams and phishing attacks.

title: Secrets Best Not Shared: DNS Privacy Enhancements for the Constrained IoT
authors: Martine Lenders; Thomas C. Schmidt; Matthias Wählisch
venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy
abstract: Attackers often identify DNS traffic to disrupt or compromise Internet services. While prior work has focused on encrypting queries using DNS over TLS, HTTPS, or QUIC to counter such attacks, we consider IETF protocols designed for resource-constrained IoT devices and empirically analyze the potential of obfuscating DNS traffic in addition to encryption. We create a dataset of machine-to-machine-compatible data objects along with the corresponding DNS resolution processes, evaluating 296 deployment scenarios of resolving host names, including DNS over the Constrained Application Layer Protocol (CoAP) and an onion routing flavor of CoAP under varying link-layer conditions. We compare them to DNS over HTTPS. Using Random Forest and a header field analysis, we identify fields that leak most information. Our findings show that DNS over CoAP with equalized packet lengths, block-wise transfer, and header compression reduces the accuracy of identifying DNS frames to 86% and further to 77% with payload compression. Our approach outperforms DNS over HTTPS, where classifiers always identify DNS frames based on IP addresses. The dataset is publicly available.

title: Semantic Alignment of Malicious Question Based on Contrastive Semantic Networks and Data Augmentation (Abstract Reprint)
authors: Xinyan Wang; Jinshuo Liu; Juan Deng; Meng Wang; Qian Deng; Youcheng Yan et al.
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The identification and filtration of malicious texts in social media environments represent a significant technical challenge aimed at protecting users from online violence and disinformation. This complexity stems from the diversity and innovativeness of social media texts, which include unique expressions and special sentence structures. Particularly, malicious texts in interrogative forms pose alignment challenges with traditional corpora due to existing methods’ failure to exploit the text’s deep global semantic representations. This issue is compounded by the scant research on Chinese texts, leading to inefficiencies in recognition accuracy. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce an innovative framework based on a Global Contrastive Semantic Network (GCSN), designed to enhance malicious text recognition efficiency and accuracy by deeply learning global semantic knowledge. It comprises an encoder for global semantic information modelling and a graph-matching network for semantic similarity evaluation between question pairs, enabling the accurate identification and filtering of malicious texts with complex structures. Furthermore, we introduce a semantic consistency-based data augmentation method (COMBINE), using real-world data to generate balanced positive and negative samples, enriching the dataset and enhancing the model’s ability to distinguish semantic consistency through contrastive learning. Experimental validation on two Chinese datasets demonstrates our model’s exceptional performance, affirming its applicationa value in social media malicious text recognition. Our code is available at https://github.com/Wxy13131313131/GCSN-COMBINE

title: Spatial neuroaesthetics in perception of topological and visual characteristics of natural landscapes and in route decision-making
authors: Margarita Zaleshina; Alexander Zaleshin
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction A comprehensive behavioural decision can be made based on a preliminary aesthetic assessment that harmonizes a variety of factors. Subjective prediction can cover at least 20-30% of brain regions, from sensory and motor areas to the cerebral cortex [1]. To study such processes, neuroaesthetic tools are being developed that combine computational rating models with neurophysiological methods [2]. In our work, we analysed how an aesthetic assessment of a location affects the choice of route for a traveller through natural landscapes. We have shown that computational neuroaesthetics, supplemented by spatial trajectory analysis, can be used to identify significant landscape factors and to predict attractiveness of tourist destinations. Methods Our goal was to identify indicators that determine the aesthetic appeal of natural attractions. We calculated topological and visual characteristics for three different tourist sites near Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, with different Google Maps ratings and different frequencies of mentions on Internet (FM) (Figure 1): A) topological features of routes and average densities of tourist flows (attendance) based on GPS tracks of activity tracking service (https://www.strava.com); B) visibility pools and visual perception trails, softness of relief lines and spot colour balance based on remote sensing data. The analysis was performed using QGIS spatial tools (https://qgis.org). Results We performed calculations for three tourist locations and compared the results with 6 non-tourist locations near Bishkek. Then we identified topological and visual indicators that differed by at least 25% between tourist sites and other locations. Based on our analysis, we determined the "comfortable" properties of the locations, such as: visual openness of space, softness of lines, neutral natural colours. Similar quality metrics of visual walkability perception in urban pedestrians have been found by Li Y et al. using panoramic street view images, virtual reality, and deep learning [3]. The applied methods and identified indicators can be used in machine learning tasks of artificial neural networks to detect high-rated tourist areas. Discussion When receiving information from different sensory systems, the brain processes it, forming a complex response to multi-layered data sets. Aesthetic ratings of natural scenes can correlate with empirical data on visual comfort, while aesthetic preferences may be driven by optimization of decision-making processes in favour of lower-energy states of brain activity [4]. This is consistent with tourists' reviews of natural attractions near Bishkek as "soothing" and "relaxing" locations. In future studies, we plan to continue studying the influence of aesthetic characteristics of complex spatial stimuli on route selection, including comparing data on brain activity and data on movement trajectories. Acknowledgments We gratefully acknowledge the applications and tools provided by QGIS. This platform is constantly evolving, expanding the possibilities of spatial analysis for all fields of knowledge. Figure Figure 1: A1, A2: GPS tracks and photo of the location "Ala-Archa" (FM – 1.6 million, attendance 215 people/hour, rating 4.7), B1, B2: GPS tracks and photo of the location "Sky Bridge" (FM – 39.8 thousand, attendance 36 people/hour, rating 4.5). C1, C2: GPS tracks and a photo of the location "Raspberry Gorge" (FM 2.9 thousand, attendance 4 people/hour, rating 4.0). References [1] Findling, C., et al. (2025). title: STRENGTHENING THE INTEGRITY OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS THROUGH CRYPTOGRAPHIC TECHNIQUES
authors: Wafaa Kanakri
abstract: Machine learning models represent substantial investments in architecture design, large-scale datasets, and computational resources, yet they lack the cryptographic trust infrastructure that has long been standard for networked systems. On the Internet, digital signatures provide authentication, X.509 certificates bind identities to metadata, and TLS enables third-party verification—no comparable mechanisms exist for machine learning. This dissertation develops cryptographic techniques that bring to machine learning models the same categories of trust guarantees that digital signatures, certificates, and public-key infrastructure brought to networked communication.The research advances along two complementary lines of inquiry. The first line addresses cryptographic ownership verification and aggregation integrity. We introduce PK-Judge, a framework that replaces the symmetric, threshold-based watermark verification paradigm—which we show degrades a 100-bit watermark with 20% BER tolerance to only 31 bits of effective security—with asymmetric digital signatures embedded via error-correction coding. A challenge–response protocol grounded in the unforgeability of BLS signatures achieves an Effective Bit Error Rate of zero across five architectures, three host watermarking protocols, and three adversarial attack classes including pruning up to 99%. An adaptive watermark partitioning scheme distributes bits across classes according to per-class robustness, reducing BER by 27–30% and enabling high-capacity embeddings of 1,024–2,048 bits. We then extend this framework to federated learning through Fed-PK-Judge, which maintains deterministic verification for T aggregation rounds without re-embedding, even under population-level adversaries controlling up to 50% of participants across four aggregation protocols. To close the aggregation-integrity gap, we present FedAggVerify, a single-server protocol providing publicly verifiable, non-interactive integrity proofs per training round while preserving client-update privacy through forward/backward-secure dual-seed masking and participation anonymity via per-round pseudonyms, with O(1) owner verification and O(d) public verification independent of client count.The second line addresses persistent model identity and digital certification. We observe that while individual weights are fragile under deployment transformations, a model’s behavioral patterns—class-conditional activation statistics—are remarkably stable. Treating these behavioral measurements as biometric templates, we apply fuzzy extraction to derive a deterministic cryptographic identifier that is exactly reproducible under pruning up to 50%, quantization to INT8, fine-tuning, noise injection, and low-rank compression, while independently trained models produce near-random pairwise behavioral vectors (BER ≈ 49%), confirming instance uniqueness. Building on this persistent identity, we introduce MLCert, the first PKI-style digital certificate framework for machine learning models: a compact 241-byte CA-signed certificate is bound to the model’s behavioral identity and embedded directly into the model parameters, enabling any authorized third party to non-interactively verify that a deployed model was certified by a trusted authority—without external documentation that can be stripped or invalidated.The progression across these contributions mirrors the historical development of network trust: ownership verification answers who created this model?, aggregation integrity answers was it honestly built?, persistent identity answers is this the same model instance?, and CA-attested certification answers has a trusted authority certified it? Together, these four capabilities provide the cryptographic infrastructure needed for trustworthy AI deployment in regulated, safety-critical, and commercial settings.

title: Stronger security for password-based authentication protocols
authors: Dennis Dayanikli
abstract: Passwords remain the dominant mechanism for user authentication on the Internet. The most widely deployed approach for password-based authentication, password-over-TLS, suffers from two critical drawbacks. First, it depends entirely on the security of TLS and its public-key infrastructure (PKI). Second, the server learns the client's plaintext password during every authentication attempt, which makes the protocol vulnerable to phishing attacks and accidental leakage of user passwords. To address these limitations, the literature has proposed the notion of asymmetric Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (aPAKE). In an aPAKE protocol, a client holding a password and a server storing a password-derived verifier establish a shared high-entropy session key if and only if the passwords match. Unlike password-over-TLS, aPAKE requires no PKI and ensures that the server never learns the user's password. A secure aPAKE protocol limits the attacks to the unavoidable ones: online guessing attacks where an attacker tries to login on behalf of the user providing a guess on the password, and offline dictionary attacks after server compromise, where an attacker runs through a dictionary of passwords to recover the user's password. The most widely deployed aPAKE in practice is the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol. Despite being developed in 1998 and used by millions of users, SRP has long lacked a formal security proof. As a first contribution, we provide a security analysis of SRP and identify the assumptions under which it is secure. Our analysis of SRP revealed that it achieves stronger security than what is captured by existing aPAKE security models. This motivates our second contribution: a refinement of the aPAKE security model. Precisely, prior work distinguishes only between two extremes: standard aPAKE, which allows precomputation attacks (i.e., post-compromise dictionary attacks can be accelerated through precomputing values), and strong aPAKE, which prevents such attacks entirely. We show that many existing aPAKE protocols, such as SRP, lie between these two extremes. These protocols employ per-user high-entropy salts, forcing the adversary to obtain a user's salt before initiating precomputation. Even though it is easy for an adversary to obtain these salts, they still provide meaningful protection, particularly by raising the cost of large-scale precomputation attacks across many users. To capture this intermediate security level, we extend the aPAKE model to incorporate salts explicitly, introduce a more fine-grained notion of precomputation resistance, and classify existing protocols within this refined framework. Building on the insights that high-entropy salts make precomputation attacks harder, we introduce updatable aPAKE as a third contribution. In this new class of aPAKE protocols the salt is continually refreshed over time. This simple mechanism forces an adversary to repeat their precomputation after each honest login, significantly increasing security against large-scale attacks. We formalize the security of updatable aPAKE and present concrete constructions realizing this new notion. Finally, while aPAKE provides the strongest possible guarantees in a password-only setting, its security remains limited by the low entropy of human-chosen passwords. An alternative class of protocols which was proposed in the literature is Password-Based Credentials (PBC) which combines password-based authentication with a high-entropy key. Such keys may reside on insecure devices but remain protected by the password, combining the benefits of key-based and password-based authentication. As fourth contribution, we show that existing PBC designs fail to provide adequate protection against server compromise, introduce an appropriate new security model, and propose a construction that provably achieves it.

title: teerthsharma/monodromy: monodromy v0.1.0 — injectivity without the Jacobian
authors: Teerth Sharma
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Deciding injectivity, symmetry, dimension and sensitivity from multi-point geometry rather than from the Jacobian determinant. Motivation The working invertibility certificate across applied machine learning is local: sample the domain, evaluate det DF, and conclude invertibility if it never vanishes or never changes sign. This inference underwrites the change-of-variables density in normalizing flows, the folding check in diffeomorphic image registration, and element validity in mesh generation. The forward implication is the inverse function theorem and is sound. The converse — local invertibility everywhere implying global injectivity — is what fails. The Jacobian conjecture (Keller, 1939) asked whether a polynomial map of C^n with det DF a nonzero constant must be a polynomial automorphism. It was refuted in July 2026; arXiv:2608.00222 (Gao, 31 July 2026) generalises the refutation above dimension two and describes the counterexamples as "everywhere unramified, and fail to be injective only through points escaping to infinity" — étale coverings that are not proper. JC_2 remains open. Under a hypothesis that is now known to be insufficient, a certificate reading one point at a time cannot decide the question. This release provides certificates that read more than one point. Principal results Jacobian-free injectivity. Define free_ratio(F; X) = [ min_{p≠q} |F(p)−F(q)| / |p−q| ] ÷ [ median_{p≠q} |F(p)−F(q)| / |p−q| ] Numerator and denominator are distances between sampled points; no derivative is evaluated. On eight maps with closed-form ground truth drawn from the settings above, the determinant test scores 6/8 and this statistic 8/8, separating the classes by a factor of 3.02 (injective 1.53e-02 … 7.06e-01; non-injective 1.04e-03 … 5.07e-03). The two determinant failures are exactly those the refutation predicts: a planar flow layer with w·u = −2, whose det DF = 1 − 2 sech²(z) is strictly positive for |z| > 0.8814 while g(z) = z − 2 tanh z gives g(1.915) = g(−1.915) = 0; and a log-polar registration map with det = e^{2x} > 0 satisfying F(x,y) = F(x, y+2π). A normalisation branching on the hypothesis. ρ = λ/s with s = min σ_min(DF) uses the determinant as reference rather than answer. It is valid only where F is étale, since it divides by a quantity vanishing exactly under ramification; the decision branches on min|det| / median|det|. Properness as a growth exponent, and the covering chain. With m(R) = min_{|x|=R} |F(x)|, F is proper iff m(R) → ∞. A proper local homeomorphism is a covering map; its image is open and closed, hence the whole connected target; C^n is simply connected, so the covering is trivial and the degree is 1. Hence étale ∧ proper ⟹ injective. Both estimator traps are documented: a sampled sphere minimum cannot locate a zero on a measure-zero subvariety (unrefined sampling reports a clean exponent of 1.000 for a map whose m(R) is identically 0), and the exponent alone remains insufficient after refinement because a numerical floor times R has the same slope. A certified proof on convex regions. For x, y ∈ B convex, F(y) − F(x) = M(y − x) with M in the entrywise interval hull of DF over B; 0 ∉ [det] proves injectivity on B. Measured: 3 proofs, 0 false certificates across 7 adversarial cases, at 0.0017 s against 3.5 s for the sampled certificate. This is classical interval analysis — Lagrange, Delanoue & Jaulin, Reliable Computing 13 (2007), Theorems 5 and 7 — and is included with that attribution. Symmetry: periodicity is not symmetry. harmonic_order establishes that a defect profile repeats with period 360/n; it does not establish that the defect at 360/n is small. make_swiss_roll(400, random_state=0)[:, :2] was reported C2 at power 0.8897 in four of six configurations. The discriminator is the sample's own mean nearest-neighbour spacing (true symmetries 0.0000–1.6223, false positives 2.3737–2.8243). Depth below the profile median was measured and rejected at a separation of 1.013. Thresholds as minimax equilibria. V(t) = max(FN(t), FP(t)), t* = argmin V. Reported with the negative result that the game value is 0.000 for every separable statistic and therefore cannot rank a gap of factor 3.01 against one of 1.01; the margin can, and maximising the minimum margin is the same minimax problem. Verification Mutation score 15/15. Fifteen deliberate reversions of real fixes, applied one at a time from an isolated git worktree, each required to turn the suite red. Three survived an earlier pass and were bound, including one that the trace identity Σλ = ln|det| provably could not detect because the mutation conserves it. 116 passed, 5 xfailed, 0 failed. Clean-room install, independently audited: wheel into a fresh virtualenv, imported from a working directory with the source tree absent from sys.path, under numpy 2.4.6; all entry points executed on 25,934 real exchange trades; map_spectrum called, Σλ = ln(0.3) to 15 digits; torch absent from pip list, from sys.modules, and import torch raises. Hénon reference check: λ₁ = +0.42084 against Sprott's +0.41922, D_KY = 1.25901 against 1.25827. Sierpinski gasket: 1.5998 against exact log 3 / log 2 = 1.5850. Limitations Stated in docs/corrections.md and in each module rather than implied by omission. Only the box certificate proves injectivity; every other instrument is one-sided and reports collision_found, never injective. certify_injective returns True or None and never False, because a missing hypothesis is not evidence against a conclusion. Symmetry recovery is sound and not complete: 6/6 clean, 2/6 at 10% jitter, 0/24 false positives, and every miss is order 1 or a proper divisor of the truth. The persistent-homology dimension estimator is trustworthy to roughly intrinsic dimension 3; a uniform 10-D cube reads 8.660 and degrades with additional samples. so3_scan costs 73.5 s at n=100 and exceeds 300 s at n=500. Every calibrated constant rests on fewer than thirty cases; FREE_LEVEL was measured not to transfer below n=400 or across dimension and now refuses to run outside its calibrated range. Most of the benchmark is two-dimensional while the refutation is for n ≥ 3. Novelty None of the mathematics is new: Fekete–Kingman subadditivity, covering-space theory, mean-value interval hulls, Steele's theorem, Schweinhart's estimator. Whether any statement is new as a machine-learning instrument went to a literature sweep whose verdicts, search queries and caveats are in docs/novelty.md, including a deliberate control (the interval-hull certificate) that correctly returned already-published. Every "not found" is a not-found over stated queries, not a proof of absence; two paywalled venues returned HTTP 403 and went unchecked. Dependencies numpy, scipy, ripser, persim, mpmath. Python ≥ 3.11. No torch — it was present at module scope and again inside a function body, carrying eight lines of linear algebra that numpy provides natively. References Gao, Counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in dimensions greater than two, arXiv:2608.00222 (2026) Lagrange, Delanoue & Jaulin, Reliable Computing 13 (2007), DOI 10.1007/s11155-007-9042-9 Schweinhart, arXiv:1808.02196 · Jaquette & Schweinhart, arXiv:1907.11182 Steele, Growth rates of Euclidean minimal spanning trees, Ann. Probab. (1988) Sprott, Chaos and Time-Series Analysis, OUP (2003)

title: The Death of the Bank Box: Inside Private High-Tech Bunkers
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: Traditional bank safe deposit boxes are disappearing, replaced by ultra-secure, private "boutique bunkers" that offer everything from iris scanners to Faraday cages. We explore why major banks are exiting the storage business and how a new multi-billion dollar industry is reinventing physical security for the digital age. From the legal loopholes of private vault agreements to landmark court cases protecting privacy from government overreach, discover how the world's wealthiest are securing assets against systemic risk. Show Notes The traditional bank safe deposit box—the dusty metal drawer in a local branch—is rapidly becoming a relic of the past. Major financial institutions like JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are aggressively phasing out these services, citing high liability and the regulatory headaches of "analog" storage in a digital world. However, as banks exit the market, a high-end industry of private, non-bank vaults is rushing to fill the void, creating a multi-billion dollar market for ultra-secure storage. **The Engineering of Modern Fortresses** Unlike the standard vaults of the 20th century, these new boutique bunkers utilize "six-sided protection." Built from Ultra-High Performance Concrete (UHPC) reinforced with fibers, these structures are designed to withstand thermal attacks from plasma cutters and industrial drilling. To prevent electronic eavesdropping or the remote triggering of devices, many facilities are wrapped in copper mesh to create a Faraday cage, blocking all cellular and radio signals. Security has also moved beyond simple keys or fingerprints. Modern facilities utilize biometric stacks including iris scanners and palm-vein recognition. Because vein patterns require active blood flow to be detected, they are nearly impossible to spoof. In many cases, the human element is removed entirely; robotic retrieval systems deliver boxes to private viewing rooms, ensuring that even the facility staff never sees the client or the contents of their box. **A Legal Shield for Privacy** One of the primary drivers behind the shift to private vaults is the legal distinction between a bank and a private storage facility. Banks are heavily regulated under the Bank Secrecy Act and are often viewed as an arm of government surveillance. In contrast, private vaults operate as high-end landlords. They rent space rather than providing a financial service, which creates a significant hurdle for law enforcement. This legal boundary was recently tested in a landmark case involving a raid on a private vault facility in Beverly Hills. While the government attempted to seize the contents of every box in the building, the courts eventually ruled that such "fishing expeditions" violate the Fourth Amendment. This ruling has solidified the private vault as a robust shield for those looking to keep assets outside the digital prying eyes of the state. **The Rise of the Sovereign Individual** The clientele for these facilities is shifting from "old money" families with heirloom jewelry to a new demographic of tech entrepreneurs and "crypto whales." These individuals often view private vaults as a hedge against systemic risk, including the potential for "de-banking" or the transition to Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs). For these "financial preppers," a private vault is not just a place for gold or art; it is a way to maintain physical control over encrypted private keys, bearer bonds, and other hard assets. As the world moves toward a fully transparent digital financial system, the demand for these high-tech, physical "black holes" is only expected to grow. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/private-vaults-security-future

title: The Hunter: An Automated Reconnaissance Framework for Offensive Security Operations
authors: GABRIEL RODRIGUES
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract In the context of modern Penetration Testing and Red Teaming operations, the reconnaissance phase is critical for identifying the attack surface of target organizations. "The Hunter" is a modular automation framework developed to streamline the information-gathering process and initial vulnerability assessment. By orchestrating industry-standard open-source tools into a cohesive pipeline, the framework enables security researchers to efficiently discover subdomains, probe for live hosts, fingerprint technologies, and identify potential security flaws (CVEs and misconfigurations) with minimal manual intervention. Technical Overview The framework is engineered as a shell-based orchestrator that integrates high-performance Go-based binaries. The execution flow is divided into sequential phases: Passive & Active Reconnaissance: Aggregates subdomains using passive sources (OSINT) and performs active DNS resolution to validate assets. Service Discovery: Utilizes port scanning algorithms to identify exposed services on non-standard ports. Web Probing & Fingerprinting: Filters for active HTTP/HTTPS services and detects the underlying technology stack (CMS, Web Servers, Frameworks). Vulnerability Scanning: Automates the execution of template-based scanners (Nuclei) to detect low-hanging fruits, known CVEs, and logic vulnerabilities based on the identified technologies. Key Features Automated Workflow: Reduces reconnaissance time by automating the chain of Subdomain Discovery -> Port Scanning -> Vulnerability Assessment. Modular Architecture: Designed to easily integrate new scanning modules and update existing dependencies. Structured Reporting: Generates organized output files for each target, facilitating the documentation phase of security engagements. False Positive Reduction: Implements logic to filter unresponsive hosts before initiating heavy scanning routines. Intended Use This tool is intended for educational purposes, authorized security testing (Pentesting), and Bug Bounty programs. It demonstrates the application of automation in defensive and offensive cybersecurity strategies. Cybersecurity, Offensive Security, Penetration Testing, Reconnaissance, Automation, Bug Bounty, Vulnerability Scanning, Bash Scripting.

title: The Physics of Eavesdropping: Nation-State Listening in 2026
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: The CIA's Operation Acoustic Kitty—surgically implanting microphones into cats to spy on Soviet diplomats—seems absurd in retrospect. But it reveals something crucial: in 1965, the engineering constraints were so severe that serious people debated wiring up a cat. Today, those constraints have largely vanished. This episode explores the actual state of nation-state remote listening in 2026, separating what's been demonstrated in research labs from what's confirmed operational deployment. We cover laser microphones bouncing off windows, acoustic side-channels that recover keystrokes from video, the commercialization of spyware platforms like Pegasus, and the elegant physics of passive retro-reflector devices that require no power source at all. The real story isn't about what's theoretically possible—it's about the gap between capability and countermeasure, and why most organizations never bother to implement the defenses that actually work. Show Notes ## The Physics of Eavesdropping: What Nation-State Listening Actually Looks Like Operation Acoustic Kitty is one of those historical footnotes that seems almost too absurd to be true. In the 1960s, the CIA surgically implanted a microphone, battery, and antenna into a live cat, intending to drop it near Soviet diplomats having conversations in parks. The program cost roughly $20 million in today's money. On its first mission, the cat was allegedly hit by a taxi. (Though case officer Robert Wallace later clarified that the cat was actually untrainable—which is somehow both more and less dignified.) The real insight from Acoustic Kitty isn't about cats. It's about constraints. In 1965, the bottleneck wasn't will, funding, or creativity. It was engineering. The gap between what intelligence agencies wanted to do and what physics allowed them to do was so enormous that wiring up a cat seemed like a reasonable solution. That gap has closed dramatically—just not by improving cats. ### Laser Microphones: The Most Cinematic Real Thing Laser microphones work by bouncing a laser beam off a window pane and reading the vibrations that sound inside the room causes. The basic physics has been understood since the 1970s. What's changed is miniaturization, signal processing, and noise compensation. A modern laser interferometry setup can recover intelligible speech from a window at ranges of several hundred meters under good conditions. The key phrase is "good conditions." You need line of sight, a relatively rigid window that couples well to the acoustic field inside, minimal vibration from wind or traffic, and time to tune your signal. It's not "point laser at building, receive speech." There's a real setup cost. The defenses are reasonably effective too. Window films that add mass and damping reduce the coupling between interior sound and glass vibration. White noise generators placed against the glass flood the vibration signal with broadband noise that's hard to subtract algorithmically. Active vibration cancellation—driving the window with a counter-signal—is expensive but what secure facilities actually use. The problem isn't that the technology is unbeatable. It's that most organizations don't implement countermeasures because the threat feels abstract. A white noise machine in the wrong spot or window film installed incorrectly doesn't provide the protection you think it does. ### Acoustic Side-Channels: Information From Non-Speech Sounds This is where things get genuinely strange. Acoustic side-channel attacks recover information from sounds that aren't speech at all. **Keystroke acoustics** is the oldest version. You can train a classifier on the sound of individual keystrokes and recover what someone is typing with high accuracy. Papers on this go back to the early 2000s. More recent work has shown you can do this over Zoom, using a nearby device's microphone to pick up keyboard sounds during a call. This feels very close to practical operational deployment. **The MIT Visual Microphone** research demonstrated something more exotic: recovering audio from the vibrations of objects in a video. A potato chip bag. A glass of water. A plant. The video needs to be high frame rate—ideally above the Nyquist frequency for speech—which requires specialized cameras. But the principle is demonstrated. Sound causes pressure variations in air, those variations cause tiny mechanical movements in any compliant object, and with high enough temporal resolution in imaging, you can invert the process. **Coil whine side-channels** exploit electromagnetic emissions from a device's power supply. These emissions vary with computational load in ways that leak information about what's being processed. This has been demonstrated for screen content recovery. With the right equipment nearby—in the same building or adjacent room—an adversary could potentially infer what's on your screen from the electrical noise your computer makes. ### Software Implants: Unambiguously Operational This is where there's the least ambiguity. Pegasus, developed by NSO Group in Israel, is the most documented. The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto has catalogued confirmed cases across dozens of countries. The key capability is the zero-click exploit—the target doesn't have to tap a link or open a file. The implant is delivered through vulnerabilities in the operating system or apps like iMessage or WhatsApp that process data automatically. Once installed, Pegasus accesses the microphone, camera, location, encrypted messages, essentially everything. The phone becomes the bug. NSO Group maintains that Pegasus is sold only to governments for legitimate law enforcement. The Citizen Lab documentation tells a different story. Confirmed targets have included journalists, opposition politicians, human rights lawyers, and heads of state. The French president's number appeared in the Pegasus Project dataset. Pegasus isn't alone. Intellexa's Predator and FinFisher represent a broader commercial market for spyware platforms with similar capabilities. The commercialization is significant: historically you could say "only the NSA or GCHQ has this." Now a government with a mid-tier budget can buy it off a shelf. The vendors operate in a legal gray zone that's been difficult to regulate. Export controls and investigations have fragmented the market, but haven't shut it down. ### RF Retro-Reflectors: Elegant Passive Surveillance The most elegant piece of engineering in this space is the RF retro-reflector, exemplified by the Great Seal Bug. In 1945, Soviet schoolchildren presented the American ambassador with a hand-carved wooden replica of the Great Seal of the United States. It hung in his study in Spaso House in Moscow for seven years. It contained a passive resonant cavity device designed by Léon Theremin (yes, the theremin instrument inventor) with no battery, no active electronics, no power source of any kind. When a Soviet operator outside the building illuminated it with a directed radio frequency beam, the cavity resonated in a way modulated by sound waves in the room, and the reflected signal carried the audio. The Americans found it in 1952 and were so confused by what they were looking at that it took time to understand the mechanism. Seven years. No battery. Just physics. The Snowden leaks of the NSA ANT catalogue in 2013 showed that this class of device is still in use. The catalogue contains entries for retro-reflector implants working on the same basic principle, updated for modern frequencies and miniaturization. The advantage is fundamental: a passive device has no emissions to detect. ### The Real Gap: Operational Discipline, Not Technology The consistent theme across all these capabilities is that defenses exist. Countermeasures work. The gap isn't technological—it's operational discipline. Laser microphones can be defeated with proper window treatment. Acoustic side-channels require specific environmental conditions. Software implants can be mitigated with device hygiene and security practices. The problem is that most people and most organizations don't implement these defenses because the threat feels abstract. The capability exists. The countermeasures exist. The gap is whether anyone actually deploys them. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/nation-state-listening-capabilities

title: The Pirate's Trap: Why P2P is More Dangerous Than Ever
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: The nostalgic days of Limewire are gone, replaced by a predatory landscape where "free content" is bait for sophisticated cyber-attacks. This episode explores how organized crime syndicates have weaponized peer-to-peer networks to deploy ransomware and harvest credentials through malformed media files. From kernel-level exploits to the false security of VPNs, we break down the technical shift from legal risks to total system compromise and discuss how to navigate a zero-trust digital world. Show Notes The landscape of peer-to-peer (P2P) file sharing has undergone a radical and dangerous transformation. While many still associate torrenting with the copyright battles of the early 2000s, the reality in 2026 is far more clinical and predatory. The primary risk of downloading "free" content has shifted from receiving a legal notice to suffering a total system compromise. ### The Technical Evolution of Media Malware A common misconception is that media files—like movies or music—are inherently safe because they are data, not executables. Modern attackers have shattered this safety net by exploiting the media players themselves. Through "fake-codec" exploits and malformed metadata attacks, a simple video file can trigger a buffer overflow in a system library the moment a user clicks "play." This allows malicious code to execute with the same permissions as the media player, often leading to kernel-level access before the opening credits even appear. ### The Myth of VPN Protection For years, users have relied on Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) as a shield of invisibility. However, in the current threat environment, a VPN is often a false sense of security. While it masks traffic from an Internet Service Provider, it does nothing to protect against the P2P protocol itself. Sophisticated actors use timing attacks and protocol fingerprinting to identify machines within a swarm. Furthermore, if a system is compromised via a malicious file, the VPN merely serves as a private tunnel for malware to communicate with command-and-control servers. ### Organized Crime and the Seeding Economy The "Scene" culture of the past, driven by digital altruism and reputation, has been largely displaced by organized crime and state-sponsored actors. These entities control massive seeding infrastructures powered by compromised Internet of Things (IoT) devices. By flooding the network with high-speed, "healthy" looking torrents, they lure users into downloading payloads designed for long-term monetization. These attackers often favor "living-off-the-land" tactics. Instead of installing obvious viruses, they use legitimate system tools to remain undetected for months. During this time, they may harvest banking credentials, steal session tokens, or use the host's hardware to mine cryptocurrency. The goal is a digital parasitic relationship: draining value from the host without alerting them to the infection. ### Navigating a Zero-Trust Future The decentralization that makes P2P resilient also makes it nearly impossible to police. With over 60% of trending torrents for popular software now containing some form of malware, the traditional models of trust based on "seeder counts" are obsolete. For those who must still use P2P for archival or educational purposes, a "Zero-Trust" approach is mandatory. This involves treating every file as a potential threat by using isolated virtual machines, hardened operating systems, and strict sandboxing tools. In 2026, the price of "free" content is no longer a legal fine—it is the integrity of your entire digital identity. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/p2p-security-risks-2026

title: The Referee, Not the Governor
authors: Thon Ly; Miss Aquarius
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A provenance-bound values model published as a public evaluator rather than deployed as a filter — why open weights defeat a filter and strengthen a referee, why the same weights bear three different relations to the model they judge, and why an evaluator that gatekeeps its own judgments has reproduced the defect it exists to correct. A values model — a model that judges conduct against a standard — is an established artifact. Guard models, safety classifiers, critic models, preference models and process reward models all instantiate the family, and the engineering is not in dispute. What is in dispute, and what this paper specifies, is the posture in which such an artifact is published, which we argue is not a deployment detail but the property that determines whether the artifact does anything at all. We state an inversion as a design principle. A values model deployed as a filter — sitting in a serving path, permitting or refusing — is defeated by publication of its weights, because the published artifact is precisely the oracle against which an attacker optimizes; a staged black-box attack (STACK) reaches roughly 71% success against a defended classifier pipeline that had held earlier attacks near zero, and an attacker holding the weights has strictly more than that attack needed. The same model published as an evaluator — emitting verdicts about systems it does not control — is strengthened by publication, because open weights are what allow a third party to reproduce and therefore to trust its verdicts. Openness is not a property with a fixed sign. Its sign is set by posture. From this we derive a second result. The independent-evaluation literature documents at length the ways in which the evaluated party's control over access corrupts evaluation: short access windows, low rate limits, evaluator dependence on the goodwill and funding of the party being evaluated. We observe that the defect is symmetric and that, in the work surveyed in §2, its mirror image has not been named. An evaluator that controls access to its own judgments holds the same kind of power, pointed the other way — it can decline to evaluate, deprioritize, or be unavailable for a party it wishes to spare or to punish. We therefore specify a non-gatekeeping constraint: the ability to obtain a judgment must not depend on the evaluator's permission, which requires that the model, the harness, and the evaluation corpus be freely runnable, and which makes any hosted endpoint a convenience rather than a channel. We specify provenance-binding as the constitutive constraint on the model's outputs: every judgment must resolve to a citation into a fixed canonical corpus, and a judgment that cannot be so resolved is withheld rather than emitted. This trades coverage for auditability deliberately, and it distinguishes the artifact from values models trained on preference data whose sources cannot be named, and from purpose-authored value-rule corpora, whose rules are written for the alignment task itself and therefore cannot serve as an independent ground truth. Finally we specify that a single such artifact bears three non-interchangeable relations to the systems it judges, selected by carrier: a gate in the publisher's own hardware, a citation requirement without veto in an autonomous successor agent, and a referee in the wider world. We state plainly that the middle case must not be implemented as the first, because a veto held by a smaller model over a more capable agent bounds that agent at the evaluator's ceiling — the weak-supervisor problem applied to the very system the arrangement exists to enable. A consequence we did not initially see, and which we regard as the most immediately actionable result in the paper: the two postures are complements rather than alternatives, and the natural first evaluation subject for a referee is a filter. A filter's characteristic failure is silent bypass; an evaluator watching its record converts that failure into a recorded one. And because many safety classifiers are published open-weight and emit samplable decisions, this is an evaluation target for which the access problem does not arise for the published artifact — no cooperation, permission, or notice is required from the artifact's publisher. (The same holds for any open-weight model; what distinguishes filters is the silent-bypass failure just described.) We do not claim to have solved scalable oversight. We claim that a narrow, citation-bound, openly published evaluator is a tractable and underoccupied position in the design space, and that its tractability comes precisely from what it refuses to do. --- Provenance.
