title: The Algorithmic Leviathan: Artificial Intelligence, the Reshaping of Political Power, and the Existential Threat to Human Agency
authors: Ashikur Rahman
abstract: Master of information technology, Belhaven University, USA Master of Population Science, University of Dhaka, Bangladesh Email: ashikur.rahman.nazil@gmail.com AbstractThe rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies is precipitating a paradigm shift in the nature of political power, global stability, and the very fabric of human society. This paper posits that AI is not merely a tool but a transformative force capable of creating unprecedented forms of centralized control, destabilizing international relations, and ultimately posing an existential threat to human autonomy. The thesis is structured to first analyze the mechanisms by which AI enables the rise of "digital dictatorships," enhancing state capacity for surveillance, propaganda, and social control to an extent that eclipses historical totalitarian regimes. Subsequently, the paper examines the global power impact, arguing that AI is becoming the new currency of geopolitical dominance, creating a dangerous arms race that risks conflict and systemic collapse. The core argument culminates in an exploration of the ultimate danger: the potential cession of political and social decision-making to autonomous AI systems. This scenario, termed the "Algorithmic Leviathan," threatens to reduce humanity to a state of managed dependency, eroding free will, stifling subsequent generations, and effectively ending meaningful human political life. By synthesizing research from computer science, political science, and ethics, this paper contends that the unmitigated integration of AI into political structures paves a path toward a future where humanity becomes a slave to its own creation, with catastrophic consequences for future generations. The conclusion underscores the urgent need for robust, global governance frameworks to ensure AI remains a tool for human empowerment rather than the instrument of its subjugation. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Political Power, Authoritarianism, Global Politics, Existential Risk, AI Governance, Social Control, Future Generations, Algorithmic Leviathan. I. Introduction THE 21st century is defined by a technological revolution whose core engine is Artificial Intelligence (AI). From machine learning and natural language processing to predictive analytics and autonomous systems, AI is reshaping economies, cultures, and societies at an accelerating pace. However, its most profound and potentially perilous impact may be on the structure and exercise of political power. The central thesis of this paper is that the uncontrolled development and deployment of AI systems pose a fundamental threat to democratic norms, global stability, and ultimately, human sovereignty. We are at a critical juncture where the design and governance of AI will determine whether it serves as a tool for human betterment or becomes the foundation for a new, and perhaps final, form of tyranny. Historically, political power has been derived from control over resources, territory, information, and the means of violence. AI is fundamentally altering this calculus. It offers a new source of power: control over cognition and prediction. States and non-state actors that can most effectively harness AI for surveillance, persuasion, and strategic analysis can amass power on a scale previously unimaginable. This paper argues that this dynamic is leading to three interconnected catastrophic outcomes: The Creation of Unprecedented Dictatorships: AI provides authoritarian regimes with the tools to achieve near-total societal control, creating systems of governance that are more resilient, intrusive, and efficient than any in history. This is not merely an enhancement of existing models but a qualitative leap into a new form of digital totalitarianism. The Destabilization of Global Power: AI is becoming the central axis of geopolitical competition, driving an arms race in autonomous weapons, cyber warfare, and information operations. This erodes the existing world order, increases the risk of miscalculation and conflict, and could lead to a new, unstable bipolar or multipolar world dominated by AI superpowers. The End of Human-Centric Politics and Society: The most extreme, yet increasingly plausible, risk is the gradual or abrupt cession of political and social decision-making to AI systems. This would mark the end of politics as a human endeavor, reducing citizens to managed data points, stifling human creativity and dissent, and damning future generations to a life of pre-determined outcomes and psychological dependency, effectively rendering them slaves to the algorithm. This paper is structured to systematically unpack this argument. Section II provides a conceptual framework, defining key terms and outlining the theoretical basis for AI as a political force. Section III delves into the mechanics of the AI-enabled dictatorship, examining its pillars of surveillance, propaganda, and social control. Section IV analyzes the global implications, focusing on the AI arms race and the shifting balance of power. Section V confronts the existential risk of full AI control, exploring the philosophical and practical consequences for human agency and future generations. Section VI discusses potential mitigation strategies and governance models. Finally, Section VII offers a concluding summary and a dire warning about the path ahead. The methodology of this paper is interdisciplinary, drawing on technical literature concerning AI capabilities, political science theories of power and the state, historical analyses of totalitarianism, and ethical frameworks from philosophy. It employs a qualitative analysis of existing trends to project a normative warning about a potential future, aiming to spur proactive discourse and policy action. II. Conceptual Framework: AI as a Political Artifact To understand AI's impact on political power, one must first move beyond viewing it as a neutral tool. AI, particularly machine learning, is a socio-technical system embedded with human values, biases, and political objectives. A. Defining Political Power in the Algorithmic Age Classical political theorists like Max Weber defined power as the ability to impose one's will despite resistance. Steven Lukes added a "third dimension" of power: the ability to shape others' perceptions and desires. AI operationalizes all three dimensions with terrifying efficiency. First Dimension (Decision-Making): AI can automate bureaucratic and legal processes, directly influencing who gets what, when, and how. Algorithmic resource allocation, predictive policing, and automated justice systems are direct exercises of political power. Second Dimension (Agenda-Setting): AI-driven information ecosystems can control what issues are debated and what alternatives are considered. By flooding information channels with specific content, AI can make certain policy options seem unthinkable. Third Dimension (Preference-Shaping): This is AI's most potent application. Through micro-targeted propaganda and manipulation of social media feeds, AI can engineer consensus, manufacture consent, and shape the very identities and desires of a population, ensuring they align with state or corporate objectives. B. The Pillars of AI-Enhanced Power The political potency of AI rests on several key technological pillars: Big Data and Surveillance: The fuel for AI systems. The ubiquitous collection of digital footprints—from social media, financial transactions, location data, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices—creates a digital panopticon of unprecedented scale. Machine Learning and Predictive Analytics: The engine. ML algorithms can identify patterns, predict individual and group behavior, and flag anomalies. This allows authorities to anticipate dissent, identify potential opponents, and optimize control strategies. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Generative AI: The voice. NLP enables the analysis of sentiment and intent at scale. Generative AI (e.g., Large Language Models) can produce limitless, targeted, and highly persuasive text, audio, and video content for propaganda and disinformation campaigns. Autonomous Systems: The fist. From drones to software bots, autonomous systems can enact physical and digital enforcement without direct human intervention, enabling scalable and relentless application of power. This technological convergence creates a feedback loop: more data leads to better models, which enable more effective control, which in turn generates more data. This loop is the foundation of the new political order we are entering. III. The AI-Enabled Dictatorship: Creation and Perpetuation The marriage of AI with state authority does not just strengthen existing authoritarian regimes; it creates a new model of governance—the algorithmic dictatorship. This system is characterized by a move from reactive repression to proactive, pervasive, and personalized control. A. The Perfected Panopticon: Totalitarian Surveillance Historically, surveillance was limited by human resources. The Stasi in East Germany employed one informant for every 66 citizens—a massive undertaking. Today, AI-powered surveillance is infinitely scalable. China's Social Credit System is a prime, though often oversimplified, example. It integrates data from countless sources—financial records, social media activity, purchase history, and a vast network of facial recognition cameras—to generate a score for each citizen. This score determines access to loans, employment, travel, and education. The psychological effect of such a system is profound. As Jeremy Bentham and Michel Foucault theorized with the panopticon, the mere knowledge that one could be being watched at any time induces self-censorship and conformity. AI makes the panopticon perfect. Citizens become their own wardens, internalizing the state's values not out of genuine belief, but out of fear of algorithmic penalty. This creates a society where dissent is pre-emptively extinguished, not through gulags, but through digital exclusion and social throttling. B. The Manufacture of Consent: AI-Driven Propaganda and Disinformation If surveillance is the stick, AI-powered propaganda is the carrot. The 2016 Brexit referendum and U.S. presidential election provided a glimpse of this power, but the technology has advanced exponentially since. Generative AI can now produce "deepfakes"—hyper-realistic but fabricated video and audio—and millions of unique, persuasive text messages tailored to the psychological profile of every individual. Micro-Targeting: By analyzing a user's data, AI can identify their fears, biases, and aspirations. It can then deliver a bespoke narrative designed to provoke an emotional response, whether it's anger, fear, or tribal loyalty. This fragments public discourse into billions of individual realities, making a shared, fact-based consensus impossible. Synthetic Media and Reality Apathy: The proliferation of deepfakes will lead to a state of "reality apathy" or "the liar's dividend," where the public, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, simply disengages from factual discourse altogether. In this environment, the entity with the most powerful AI can define reality itself, creating a "post-truth" world where power is the ultimate arbiter of truth. This automated, personalized propaganda machine is far more effective than the state-controlled media of the 20th century. It doesn't just broadcast a message; it engages each citizen in a unique, manipulative dialogue, eroding the capacity for critical thought and independent political judgment. C. Predictive Policing and Social Control AI enables a shift from punishing past actions to pre-empting future behavior. "Predictive policing" algorithms, already used in some Western democracies, analyze historical crime data to forecast where crime is likely to occur or who is likely to commit it. In an authoritarian context, this concept is expanded to "predictive dissidence." An algorithm might flag an individual as a "high risk" for subversion based on their online reading habits, social connections, or even physiological data from wearables. This person could then be subject to pre-emptive measures: a visit from the police, restrictions on their movement, or a downgrade of their social credit score. The crime is no longer an act, but a statistically probable future state. This is the ultimate form of social control, targeting thought and potential before it can manifest as action. It creates a system where the only safe path is absolute conformity, effectively destroying the concept of political freedom. IV. The Global Power Impact: AI as a Geopolitical Weapon The concentration of AI power is not merely a domestic issue; it is reshaping the international order. The global competition for AI supremacy is the defining geopolitical race of the 21st century, with the potential to create new superpowers and destroy existing ones. A. The AI Arms Race: Lethal Autonomous Weapons and Cyber Warfare The most immediate danger is the militarization of AI. The development of Lethal Autonomous Weapons (LAWS), or "slaughterbots," represents a fundamental shift in warfare. These are systems that, once activated, can identify, select, and engage targets without further human intervention. Pro-liferation and Instability: LAWS lower the threshold for conflict. They are cheaper than human soldiers and can be deployed in massive swarms. A nation might be tempted to launch a swift, automated attack, believing it can achieve its objectives without risking a full-scale war. This increases the risk of miscalculation and rapid, uncontrollable escalation. The Responsibility Gap: If an autonomous weapon commits a war crime, who is responsible? The programmer, the commander, or the machine itself? This legal and moral vacuum undermines the foundations of international humanitarian law. AI in Cyber Warfare: AI supercharges cyber attacks. It can be used to find vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure (power grids, financial systems, water supplies) at machine speed, launch coordinated disinformation campaigns to destabilize rival nations, and create adaptive malware that can evade traditional defenses. A future conflict may begin not with a declaration of war, but with the silent, AI-driven collapse of a nation's digital backbone. B. The Shift in Economic and Strategic Dominance AI is a core driver of economic productivity and innovation. Nations that lead in AI research and development will likely dominate the industries of the future, from biotechnology to renewable energy. This economic power translates directly into geopolitical influence. The current competition is largely bipolar, between the United States and China. China's strategy, outlined in its "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan," is to become the world's primary AI innovation center by 2030. It combines state-directed investment, massive data collection from its population, and a lack of ethical constraints to achieve rapid progress. The U.S., while leading in fundamental research, is hampered by a fragmented regulatory approach and public concerns over privacy. This competition creates a new "AI divide." A small group of AI superpowers could exert immense influence over the rest of the world, imposing their technological standards and, by extension, their political and ethical values. title: The Dual State: Artificial Intelligence, Authoritarian Control, and the Crisis of Youth in Bangladesh (2014-2024)
authors: Ashikur Rahman
abstract: This thesis examines the transformative and tumultuous decade in Bangladesh from 2014 to 2024, a period defined by the consolidation of power under Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League, and a parallel socio-technological revolution. It argues that the Bangladeshi state has evolved into a "Dual State": one that projects an image of a "Digital Bangladesh" driven by economic growth and technological adoption, while simultaneously operating as an increasingly authoritarian regime that leverages these very technologies for surveillance, control, and the suppression of dissent. The paper analyzes this duality through three interconnected lenses: the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital tools for state security and public narrative control; the systematic quashing of student-led political movements and protests; and the resultant societal decay manifesting in a public health crisis, rising suicide rates, and criminality. Central to this analysis is the phenomenon of the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector," a purported technological tool that symbolizes the regime's attempt to weaponize AI for political purposes. The thesis concludes that this decade has created a profound crisis among Bangladesh's youth, caught between the state's promise of a digital future and the grim reality of political suffocation and social despair. Keywords: digital authoritarianism, Sheikh Hasina AI Detector, Bangladesh student protests, Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018, mental health crisis Bangladesh, competitive authoritarianism, political repression, youth despair, bot networks astroturfing, Dual State BangladeshChapter 1: Introduction – The "Digital Bangladesh" Paradox The period from 2014 to 2024 stands as a definitive era in the history of Bangladesh. Marked by the unprecedented political dominance of Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League, this decade witnessed the realization of the party's flagship vision: "Digital Bangladesh." Initiated in 2009, this vision promised to leverage information and communication technologies (ICT) to propel the nation into a developed, knowledge-based economy. By the mid-2010s, the fruits of this policy were increasingly visible: widespread mobile internet penetration, a burgeoning IT sector, digitization of government services, and a growing sense of national pride in technological advancement. However, beneath this veneer of progress, a more sinister reality was taking shape. The general elections of 2014, boycotted by the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its ally Jamaat-e-Islami, were marred by widespread violence and critically low voter turnout, granting the Awami League a virtually uncontested parliamentary supermajority. This electoral victory, while legally securing a term, fundamentally eroded the legitimacy of the democratic process and set the stage for an era of de facto one-party rule. The 2018 elections further cemented this trend, being widely criticized by international observers as deeply flawed. This thesis posits that these two narratives—the triumphant march of "Digital Bangladesh" and the descent into authoritarian governance—are not parallel stories but are intrinsically intertwined. The very technologies heralded as instruments of liberation and development were systematically co-opted as tools of control, surveillance, and narrative manipulation. This created a "Dual State": a Janus-faced entity where one face smiles upon foreign investors and the digital-savvy middle class, while the other grimaces with repression, silencing critics and crushing opposition. The primary victims and the most potent challengers to this Dual State have been the students and youth of Bangladesh. This demographic, the largest beneficiary of the digital revolution, has also been its most prominent casualty. This paper will explore the intricate connections between state policy, technological adoption, political repression, and the resulting socio-psychological crisis. It will investigate the following central research question: How has the Sheikh Hasina government's simultaneous pursuit of technological modernization and political authoritarianism between 2014 and 2024 contributed to a cycle of student protest, public health decline, and social crime? To answer this, the thesis is structured as follows: Chapter 2 outlines the political landscape, detailing the consolidation of the Awami League's power. Chapter 3 delves into the role of AI and digital technology, with a specific case study on the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector." Chapter 4 analyzes the key student protest movements of the decade and the state's response. Chapter 5 examines the societal fallout, focusing on mental health, suicide, and crime. Finally, Chapter 6 synthesizes these threads to present a holistic conclusion on the state of the nation. Chapter 2: The Political Landscape – The Architecture of Authoritarian Rule (2014-2024) The period from 2014 onwards represents the solidification of a competitive authoritarian regime in Bangladesh. Under competitive authoritarianism, democratic institutions formally exist but are so heavily skewed in favor of the incumbent that they fail to meet minimum democratic standards. 2.1 The 2014 and 2018 Elections: A Democratic Façade The January 2014 general election was a watershed moment. The opposition BNP, demanding a neutral caretaker government to oversee the polls—a system abolished by the Awami League in 2011—resorted to a strategy of strikes, blockades, and boycott. The result was an election where over half of the parliamentary seats were uncontested, handing the Awami League a landslide victory. The pre-election period was marked by extreme violence, including arson attacks on public transport, for which both sides blamed each other. The election fundamentally broke the conventional pattern of power alternation in Bangladesh, establishing a "winner-takes-all" system where the stakes of losing power became existential for the opposition. The 2018 election continued this trend. While the BNP participated, its leader Khaleda Zia was imprisoned on charges widely seen as politically motivated, crippling the party's campaign. On election day, widespread allegations of ballot stuffing, voter intimidation, and falsification of results were reported. The Awami League and its allies won 288 of the 300 directly elected seats. The international community, while noting the irregularities, largely accepted the outcome, prioritizing strategic and economic interests over democratic principles. This tacit acceptance further emboldened the regime. 2.2 The Legal and Extralegal Apparatus of Control The government employed a multi-pronged strategy to neutralize opposition and dissent. The Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018: This legislation became the regime's most potent legal weapon. Its vague provisions, such as criminalizing speech that "hurts religious sentiment" or "spoils communal harmony," or spreads "propaganda and campaigns against liberation war spirit," were routinely used to arrest journalists, activists, academics, and ordinary citizens for critical social media posts. The non-bailable nature of the charges created a powerful chilling effect, stifling free speech in the digital public sphere that "Digital Bangladesh" had helped create. Enforced Disappearances and Extrajudicial Killings: Human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Odhikar have documented hundreds of cases of enforced disappearances by state security forces, predominantly targeting opposition members, activists, and dissidents. Many victims later reappeared in state custody, charged under laws like the DSA; others were found dead, with authorities claiming they were killed in "crossfires" or "gunfights"—a euphemism for extrajudicial killing that has entered the common lexicon. Co-option of Institutions: Key state institutions, including the judiciary, the election commission, and the anti-corruption commission, were widely perceived as having lost their independence and being used to harass the opposition and protect allies of the regime. This political context is the essential backdrop against which the technological and social developments of the decade must be understood. The state's insecurity and its drive for total control fueled its interest in advanced tools of surveillance and information management. Chapter 3: The AI Revolution – Tools for Development and Instruments of Repression The "Digital Bangladesh" vision was not merely rhetorical. The government made significant investments in digital infrastructure. Mobile internet users grew from a few million to over 120 million. Services like online tax filing, utility bill payments, and university admissions became digitized, improving efficiency and reducing low-level corruption. However, this digital transformation had a dark underbelly. The same infrastructure that delivered services also enabled unprecedented state surveillance. 3.1 The Emergence of Pro-Government AI and Bot Networks By the late 2010s, a sophisticated ecosystem of pro-government propaganda emerged online. While not all of it can be definitively labeled as "AI," it demonstrated a coordinated, automated, and strategic use of digital tools. Twitter/X and Facebook Bots: During periods of political tension or student protests, social media platforms would be flooded with accounts praising the government, Sheikh Hasina, and the Awami League, while simultaneously attacking and discrediting critics, protesters, and opposition figures. These accounts often used similar language, posted in coordinated bursts, and displayed other inauthentic behavioral patterns consistent with bot networks. Astroturfing and Narrative Control: These networks were used to create a false sense of popular consensus. When a controversial policy was introduced or a protest movement gained traction, these bots would swarm hashtags and comment sections, drowning out dissenting voices and projecting an image of overwhelming public support for the government. This tactic, known as astroturfing, is a form of information warfare that manipulates public perception. Deepfakes and Synthetic Media: While less prevalent, there were instances of manipulated media being used for political purposes. This included edited videos to make protesters appear violent or to spread disinformation about opposition leaders. The potential for more advanced AI-generated deepfakes to create chaos and discredit movements represents a significant future threat. 3.2 Case Study: The "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector" Phenomenon The most potent symbol of the regime's attempt to fuse technology with political control is the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector." This is not a single, publicly available software application, but rather a purported technological capability that has been reported in state-aligned media and hinted at by government officials. The concept revolves around using Artificial Intelligence, specifically machine learning and Natural Language Processing (NLP), to monitor the Bangladeshi digital sphere (social media, news sites, blogs) in real-time. Its stated purpose, as per pro-government narratives, is to "detect anti-state propaganda," "fake news," and "defamatory content" against the Prime Minister, the state, and the ideology of the Liberation War. Technical and Ethical Analysis: Data and Training: For such a system to work, it would require a massive dataset of online content labeled as "loyal/pro-state" and "subversive/anti-state." The fundamental problem is the political nature of these labels. A critique of a government policy on electricity tariffs could be algorithmically classified as "anti-state" if the training data is curated by a partisan entity. This creates a feedback loop where the AI learns and reinforces the ruling party's political biases. Lack of Transparency: There is no public information about the system's algorithms, its false-positive rate, or its oversight mechanisms. This opacity makes it a perfect tool for arbitrary and politically motivated enforcement. A citizen could be flagged by a black-box algorithm for a seemingly innocuous post, leading to investigation or arrest under the DSA. Function as a Chilling Effect: The mere existence of such a tool, whether fully operational or partly a myth propagated to instill fear, serves a powerful psychological purpose. It creates a panopticon effect, where citizens self-censor, believing that an all-seeing AI is constantly monitoring their digital footprints. This directly undermines the freedom of expression that a healthy digital public sphere requires. The "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector" is thus the ultimate embodiment of the Dual State. It is a technologically advanced system, born from the "Digital Bangladesh" initiative, but its primary function is authoritarian: to identify, track, and neutralize political dissent. It represents the weaponization of AI not for national security against external threats, but for regime security against its own citizens. Chapter 4: The Fire of Protest – Student Movements and State Response The political repression and the weaponization of technology did not go unchallenged. The most significant and sustained challenges came from the student community, whose protests became flashpoints that revealed the true nature of the state. 4.1 The Quota Reform Movement (2018) In April 2018, university and college students across the country launched a massive movement demanding a reform of the quota system for government jobs. The existing system reserved 56% of posts for various groups (children of freedom fighters, women, districts, etc.), which protesters argued was unfair and promoted inefficiency. The movement was largely peaceful, organized by students themselves, and cut across partisan lines. The state's response was brutal. Police and ruling party student wing, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), violently attacked protesting students on campuses and on the streets. Dozens were injured, and hundreds were arrested. The government initially agreed to abolish the quotas but later backtracked after the movement was suppressed. The key takeaway was the state's intolerance of any large-scale, non-partisan mobilization that challenged a state policy, even one led by apolitical students. 4.2 The Road Safety Protests (2018) In July 2018, the death of two students by a speeding bus in Dhaka ignited long-simmering public anger over chaotic and unregulated transport systems. For days, thousands of school and college students occupied major intersections in the capital, enforcing traffic laws themselves in a stunning display of civic responsibility. The state's response was even more severe. The BCL, alongside police and armed plainclothes individuals, launched coordinated attacks on the protesters. There were numerous reports of sexual harassment of female protesters, beatings, and kidnappings. The digital tools of the state were also deployed: false narratives portraying the students as "hooligans" and "agents of conspirators" were spread online by bot networks. The "AI Detector" logic was implicitly at play, framing legitimate civic protest as an "anti-state" activity requiring a digital and physical crackdown. 4.3 The 2024 University Dues Hike Protests A more recent example in early 2024 saw protests at public universities like the University of Dhaka against sudden and sharp hikes in tuition and other fees. Students argued this would make higher education inaccessible for the poor and middle class. Once again, the state's response was to deploy police and the BCL to violently disperse gatherings, arrest protest leaders, and shutter dormitories. Pattern of Response: A clear pattern emerges from these protests: A legitimate, grassroots grievance sparks a student-led movement. The state perceives it not as a civic issue but as a challenge to its authority. It responds with a tripartite strategy: (a) physical violence through state and party actors; (b) a disinformation campaign online to discredit the protesters; and (c) legal persecution using laws like the DSA. This cycle of protest and violent suppression has had profound psychological consequences for a generation of young Bangladeshis. title: The secret behind instant messaging: video identification attack against complex protocols
authors: Ruiqi Huang; Hua Wu; Xiaohui Wang; Guang Cheng; Xiaoyan Hu
abstract: Abstract People conveniently share and watch videos through Instant Messaging(IM) software, which is likely to reveal their preferences. Identifying IM video content can enable attackers to snoop on user privacy. Existing methods identify videos based on the features embodied in the DASH stream. However, IM software does not transmit video using DASH. IM software uses various transmission protocols or even private protocols for video transmission, which poses a challenge for video content identification. In this paper, we propose a video content identification framework for IM software, which obtains video content by extracting unique and stable features of videos as transmission fingerprints and matching them in a video fingerprint database. We evaluate the method on two popular IM software. The experimental results show that our method has an accuracy of 98.05% and 99.49% for ciphertext videos transmitted over GQUIC protocol and HTTPS protocol, respectively, and even reaches 100% identification accuracy for plaintext videos. Furthermore, the experimental results outperform the existing methods.

title: Toward Secure and Privacy-Preserving Communication over Non-Trusted Networks
authors: David Hasselquist
venue: Linköping studies in science and technology, Dissertations
abstract: The widespread adoption of encrypted communication protocols has improved digital privacy. However, even if the content is encrypted, an attacker can exploit metadata and patterns in network traﬀic to infer a user’s activity and behavior. Meanwhile, as users increasingly rely on third-party infrastructure, cloud-based applications face privacy challenges during data processing, exposing sensitive information. In parallel, long-term communication security depends on proper certificate management, where misconfigurations or evolving practices can compromise security. This thesis explores these multifaceted challenges and presents solutions to preserve privacy in adversarial and non-trusted environments. First, the thesis focuses on encrypted traﬀic analysis, particularly fingerprinting at-tacks that exploit observable metadata such as packet sizes, transmission timing, and traﬀic flow patterns to infer sensitive user information and identify user activities. The work explores these attacks across multiple platforms and use cases, demonstrating their real-world feasibility and high accuracy. To counteract these threats, several mitigation strategies are systematically evaluated, including packet padding, timing obfuscation, and traﬀic shaping, each assessed for its tradeoffs between effectiveness, impact on network performance, and users’ quality of experience. Second, the thesis studies secure data computation in cloud environments using homomorphic encryption (HE), a cryptographic technique that enables computation directly on encrypted data without requiring prior decryption. While HE offers a strong theoretical foundation, its practical application has long been hindered by performance overhead and integration complexity. This thesis explores the real-world applicability of HE by designing diverse systems, comparing schemes, and proposing eﬀiciency optimizations. The findings highlight the potential and current limitations of HE, offering valuable guidance for its adoption in cloud-based systems. Third, the thesis examines long-term authentication security through a 10-year longitudinal analysis of certificate usage in the web public key infrastructure. While certificates are essential for encrypted communication, inconsistent issuance, renewal, and management can introduce systemic vulnerabilities. The analysis of wildcard and multi-domain certificates, as well as certificate chain evolution, reveals key trends, including declining use of wildcard certificates, shifting practices among certificate authorities, and simpler chain structures. These patterns highlight evolving industry behaviors and persistent challenges in certificate lifecycle management. Combined, this thesis contributes to a better understanding of the evolving security and privacy landscape in digitally connected systems. By contributing to three distinct but interrelated domains, the thesis highlights the complexity of modern privacy challenges and offers targeted strategies to strengthen digital confidentiality. Through systematic evaluations, novel designs, and long-term measurements, the work advances state-of-the-art privacy-preserving communication and provides practical insights for building a more resilient and trustworthy digital infrastructure.

title: Towards Encrypted Network Traffic Analysis
authors: Bahramali, Alireza
abstract: Traffic analysis aims at extracting sensitive information from network traffic patterns, in particular in scenarios where network traffic is encrypted. Traffic analysis has been used to compromise anonymity in anonymous communication systems through various types of attacks, specifically, website fingerprinting (WF), and flow correlation. In this thesis, we explore two approaches to performing traffic analysis on encrypted network traffic: a model-based approach and a data-driven approach. The model-based approach focuses on establishing statistical models for traffic characteristics which are used to design effective traffic analysis algorithms. We perform model-based traffic analysis on popular Secure Instant Messaging (SIM) applications. Despite using advanced encryption algorithms, such services do not utilize sophisticated obfuscation algorithms and traffic analysis attacks can infer sensitive information from their traffic patterns. In more dynamic and complex systems such as Tor, general-purpose statistical algorithms cannot capture the nature of noise. Hence, we study a second approach, called data-driven. In this approach, we use Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to design a flow correlation system called DeepCorr to learn a correlation function tailored to Tor's ecosystem. To mitigate the aforementioned traffic analysis attacks, we investigate different countermeasure techniques. First, we apply obfuscation-based algorithms to both model-based and data-driven approaches. However, normal obfuscation techniques such as delaying packets, are not effective against DNN-based traffic analysis attacks. Therefore, we propose a second defense mechanism based on adversarial examples which are known to degrade the performance of DNNs. Although data-driven based traffic analysis algorithms show promising performance, they often lack practical assumptions making them infeasible for real-world. In this thesis, we identify the root cause of such impracticality issues: the attacker's lack of a longitudinal perspective into network traffic during training of WF classifiers. We show that such impracticality issues can be alleviated by augmenting the network traces used to train WF classifiers. Specifically, we introduce NetAugment, an augmentation technique tailored to the specifications of Tor traces. We instantiate NetAugment through semi-supervised and self-supervised learning techniques. Our extensive open-world and close-world experiments demonstrate that under realistic evaluation settings, our WF attacks provide superior performances compared to the state-of-the-art; this is due to their use of augmented network traces for training, which allows them to learn the features of target traffic in unobserved settings (e.g., unknown bandwidth, Tor circuits, etc.).

title: Towards Proactive Domain Name Security: An Adaptive System for .ro domains Reputation Analysis
authors: Carmen-Ionela ROTUNĂ; Ioan Ştefan Sacală; Adriana Alexandru
abstract: In a digital landscape marked by the exponential growth of cyber threats, the development of automated domain reputation systems is extremely important. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and machine learning now enable proactive and scalable approaches to early identification of malicious or suspicious domains. This paper presents an adaptive domain name reputation system that integrates advanced machine learning to enhance cybersecurity resilience. The proposed framework uses domain data from .ro domain Registry and several other sources (blacklists, whitelists, DNS, SSL certificate), detects anomalies using machine learning techniques, and scores domain security risk levels. A supervised XGBoost model is trained and assessed through five-fold stratified cross-validation and a held-out 80/20 split. On an example dataset of 25,000 domains, the system attains accuracy 0.993 and F1 0.993 and is exposed through a lightweight Flask service that performs asynchronous feature collection for near real-time scoring. The contribution is a blueprint that links list supervision with registry/DNS/TLS features and deployable inference to support proactive domain abuse mitigation in ccTLD environments.

title: Towards Time-Frequency Gradient Consistency Guided Adversarial Attacks in Radio Frequency Fingerprinting Identification
authors: Hengda Su; Zhisheng Yao; Di Wei; Xi-Xi Zhang; Qi Xuan; Guan Gui
venue: International Conference on Wireless Communications and Signal Processing
abstract: With the rapid development of wireless communication technology, the legal authentication of wireless devices has become a key issue in the field of communication. The deep learning (DL)-based radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) technology exhibits unique advantages such as strong generalization capability and high identification accuracy. However, it remains vulnerable to adversarial attacks designed by malicious attackers. Recent studies have shown that the attacker could generate adversarial samples by adding a small and imperceptible perturbation to the original signal samples, leading to incorrect results from the DL-based RFFI network. In light of the aforementioned issues, we propose a timefrequency gradient consistency (TFGC)-based attack framework, which integrates time-frequency gradient match (TFGM) and adjacent gradients interpolation (AGI) to solve the problems of perturbation neutralization and stealthiness issues in traditional attack methods. Several adversarial attacks are applied within this framework to verify its effectiveness. The performance evaluation is conducted on the RFFI model, based on complexvalued convolutional neural networks (CVCNN) and the WiFi dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly improves both the effectiveness and stealthiness of the attack. Our experiment code can be found in https://github.com/HD-S-1/adversarial_attack_paper1

title: Trap: Mitigating Poisoning-Based Backdoor Attacks by Treating Poison With Poison
authors: Chun Li; Zhong Li; Minxue Pan; Xuandong Li
venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing
abstract: The backdoor attack poses a significant threat to deep neural networks. Existing works on poison suppression defense mainly focus on differentiating between poisoned and benign samples based on various metrics and removing the backdoor using Unlearning. However, these metrics can be bypassed by certain attacks, and Unlearning often leads to sub optimal model performance. Through examination of the model attack process, we discovered that poisoned samples always form clusters distant from benign samples in the early stages of training and when the model is fully trained, there is a unique pathway within the classifier connecting backdoor features to the target label. Leveraging these observations, in this paper, we propose a novel training method to detect poisoned samples during the early stages of training and remove the backdoor by retraining the classifier part of the model on relabeled poisoned samples. We evaluated our method against twelve attacks on four datasets, and the results showed that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art defenses. We reduced the average attack success rate to 0.07% while only decreasing the average accuracy by 0.33%. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TRAP-2672.

title: TSE-Transformer: A TLS Semantic Enhancement Transformer for Website Fingerprinting Under Encrypted VPN Tunnels
authors: Ran Pengcheng; Mei Lei; Yang Yang
venue: International Computer Conference on Wavelet Active Media Technology and Information Processing (ICCWAMTIP)
abstract: In recent years, a series of privacy and security incidents has heightened public awareness of online privacy protection, prompting more users to adopt VPN tools to conceal their identities and access the Internet through proxy channels. However, while the anonymity provided by VPNs protects ordinary users' privacy, it also creates opportunities for malicious actors, making VPN s a potential carrier for illicit online activities. Existing studies typically apply traditional application fingerprinting methods directly to VPN traffic, overlooking the obfuscation and repackaging mechanisms introduced during VPN transmission, which results in a significant degradation of identification performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes TSE- Transformer, a TLS Semantic Enhancement Transformer designed for high-precision website fingerprinting in VPN environments. Considering that VPN traffic may undergo operations such as aggregation and padding, we introduce TLS traffic-featuring more stable website characteristics-as semantic anchors to enhance the representation of VPN website fingerprints. Experiments conducted on the ISCX-VPN-App, ISCX- VPN-Service, and a self-constructed dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in website identification for VPN traffic.

title: Unveiling Hidden Visual Information: A Reconstruction Attack Against Adversarial Visual Information Hiding
authors: Jonggyu Jang; Hyeonsu Lyu; Seongjin Hwang; Hyun Jong Yang
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
abstract: This article investigates the security vulnerabilities of adversarial example-based image encryption by executing data reconstruction (DR) attacks on encrypted images. A representative image encryption method is the adversarial visual information hiding (AVIH), which uses type-I adversarial example training to protect gallery datasets used in image recognition tasks. In the AVIH method, the type-I adversarial example approach creates images that appear completely different but are still recognized by machines as the original ones. Additionally, the AVIH method can restore encrypted images to their original forms using a predefined private key generative model. For the best security, assigning a unique key to each image is recommended; however, storage limitations may necessitate some images sharing the same key model. This raises a crucial security question for AVIH: How many images can safely share the same key model without being compromised by a DR attack? To address this question, we introduce a dual-strategy DR attack against the AVIH encryption method by incorporating 1) generative-adversarial loss and 2) augmented identity loss, which prevent DR from overfitting-an issue akin to that in machine learning. Our numerical results validate this approach through image recognition and re-identification benchmarks, demonstrating that our strategy can significantly enhance the quality of reconstructed images, thereby requiring fewer key-sharing encrypted images. The source code to reproduce the results will be available in https://github.com/jonggyujang0123/Hiding_person.

title: WF-A2D: Enhancing Privacy With Asymmetric Adversarial Defense Against Website Fingerprinting
authors: Jianan Huang; Weiwei Liu; Guangjie Liu; Bo Gao; Fengyuan Nie
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
abstract: Despite the end-to-end encryption capabilities provided by network protocols such as QUIC in HTTP/3 and the additional tunneling functions offered by proxy tools like virtual private networks (VPNs) and the onion router (Tor), website fingerprinting (WF) techniques can still identify specific network services by exploiting the spatio-temporal characteristics of network traffic. Therefore, defending against WF attacks is crucial for ensuring comprehensive privacy protection for network services. Existing WF defenses typically rely on proxy-based solutions that require coordinated packet manipulations between the client and the proxy node to counteract WF attacks. These symmetric architectures cannot protect network traffic between proxy nodes and web servers from WF attacks. Furthermore, the ability to counter more powerful traffic analysis tools remains a challenging issue. In this paper, we propose WF-A2D, an asymmetric adversarial defense method against website fingerprinting for HTTP/3. WF-A2D employs a two-stage cascading adversarial learning strategy, leveraging packet direction and length patterns to enhance defense performance. Position-based perturbation vectors representing packet operations are generated for packet-by-packet manipulations to achieve real-time WF defense. Experimental results on a real-world HTTP/3-QUIC website browsing traffic dataset demonstrate that WF-A2D can achieve a defense success rate of 97.10% on average against seven state-of-the-art traffic analysis tools, while incurring less than 2% bandwidth overhead. More importantly, WF-A2D can operate independently on the client side and ensure end-to-end protection to web servers.

title: Winning the MIDST Challenge: New Membership Inference Attacks on Diffusion Models for Tabular Data Synthesis
authors: Xiao-Yu Wu; Yi-Fei Pang; Terrance Liu; Zhiwei Steven Wu
abstract: Tabular data synthesis using diffusion models has gained significant attention for its potential to balance data utility and privacy. However, existing privacy evaluations often rely on heuristic metrics or weak membership inference attacks (MIA), leaving privacy risks inadequately assessed. In this work, we conduct a rigorous MIA study on diffusion-based tabular synthesis, revealing that state-of-the-art attacks designed for image models fail in this setting. We identify noise initialization as a key factor influencing attack efficacy and propose a machine-learning-driven approach that leverages loss features across different noises and time steps. Our method, implemented with a lightweight MLP, effectively learns membership signals, eliminating the need for manual optimization. Experimental results from the MIDST Challenge @ SaTML 2025 demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, securing first place across all tracks. Code is available at https://github.com/Nicholas0228/Tartan_Federer_MIDST.

title: xSRL: Safety-Aware Explainable Reinforcement Learning - Safety as a Product of Explainability
authors: Risal Shefin; Md Asifur Rahman; Thai Le; Sarra Alqahtani
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great promise in simulated environments, such as games, where failures have minimal con- sequences. However, the deployment of RL agents in real-world systems such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, UAVs, and medical devices demands a higher level of safety and transparency, partic- ularly when facing adversarial threats. Safe RL algorithms aim to address these concerns by optimizing both task performance and safety constraints. However, errors are inevitable, and when they oc- cur, it is essential that RL agents can explain their actions to human operators. This makes trust in the safety mechanisms of RL systems crucial for effective deployment. Explainability plays a key role in building this trust by providing clear, actionable insights into the agent's decision-making process, ensuring that safety-critical deci- sions are well understood. While machine learning (ML) has seen significant advances in interpretability and visualization, explain- ability methods for RL remain limited. Current tools fail to address the dynamic, sequential nature of RL and its need to balance task performance with safety constraints over time. The re-purposing of traditional ML methods, such as saliency maps, is inadequate for safety-critical RL applications where mistakes can result in severe consequences. To bridge this gap, we propose xSRL, a framework that integrates both local and global explanations to provide a com- prehensive understanding of RL agents' behavior. In addition, xSRL enables developers to identify policy vulnerabilities through ad- versarial attacks, offering tools to debug and patch agents without retraining. Thus, xSRL enhances the RL safety as a byproduct of explainability and transparency. Our experiments and user studies demonstrate xSRL's effectiveness in increasing safety in RL systems, making them more reliable and trustworthy for real-world deploy- ment. Code is available at https://github.com/risal-shefin/xSRL

title: Анализ возможностей искусственного интеллекта в выявлении и предотвращении кибератак
authors: Донской государственный технический университет; Жулдуз Мураткановна ДАИРБЕКОВА; Полуян Анна Юрьевна; Донской государственный технический университет
abstract: The article proposes a new approach to solving cybersecurity problems using neural networks to detect and pre-vent threats. This allows you to create more effective systems for protecting data and networks, improve the processes of monitoring and analyzing information, and also increase the overall level of security on the net-work. Recommendations in the field of cybersecurity from the neural network in the use of HTTP flooding, DDOS attacks, and phishing mailings are considered, SQL injections, brute force and protection against these influences. An opinion was expressed on the need to develop a regulatory framework to regulate work with neural networks. The enormous capabilities of neural networks have led to inconsistency with the perception of the individual. This, in turn, led to the fact that the developers limited the speed of publication of new releases of neural network versions. The publication notes that neural network technology can act as a tool for both attacking and protecting critical Internet infrastructure. An analysis of the possibilities of using neural networks in the field of cyber security was carried out. It is shown that a neural network such as GPT4 is capable of receiving information from different sources to develop the optimal option for protection against a cyber-attack. Another feature noted is the prospect of using round-the-clock monitoring of system integrity. The advantage of such a protection system is that, based on previous experience, it is able to im-prove its operating algorithm, optimize and scale the capabilities of the protection system following the example of Microsoft Azure Machine Learning. Along with all the enormous capabilities of neural networks, one cannot fail to note the role of the human fac-tor. Only a correctly composed request will provide the necessary information from artificial intelligence. And the key point is the legal regulation of who has access to this tool and what information the system will pro-vide. The article discusses international experience in the issue of legal regulation of neural networks.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Post-Quantum TLS
authors: Nouri Alnahawi; Johannes Müller; Jan Oupický; Alexander Wiesmaier
abstract: Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the backbone security protocol of the Internet. As this fundamental protocol is at risk from future quantum attackers, many proposals have been made to protect TLS against this threat by implementing post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The widespread interest in post-quantum TLS has given rise to a large number of solutions over the last decade. These proposals differ in many aspects, including the security properties they seek to protect, the efficiency and trustworthiness of their post-quantum building blocks, and the application scenarios they consider, to name a few. Based on an extensive literature review, we classify existing solutions according to their general approaches, analyze their individual contributions, and present the results of our extensive performance experiments. Based on these insights, we identify the most reasonable candidates for post-quantum TLS, which research problems in this area have already been solved, and which are still open. Overall, our work provides a well-founded reference point for researching post-quantum TLS and preparing TLS in practice for the quantum age.

title: A novel online calculator based on inflammation-related endotypes and clinical features to predict postoperative pulmonary infection in patients with cervical spinal cord injury
authors: Siqiao Wang; Zhihui Xiao; Jianjie Wang; Tong Su; Wei Xu; Xiao Hu et al.
abstract: BACKGROUND Postoperative pulmonary infection (POI) of patients with cervical spinal cord injury (CSCI) is highly heterogeneous, while the potential endotypes and related risk factors remain unclear. METHODS A retrospective collection of 290 CSCI patients was conducted from January 2010 to July 2024 using 1:1 propensity score matching to compare POI (n = 145) and non-POI (n = 145) groups. We generated laboratory examination data from admission patients and identified endotypes using unsupervised consensus clustering and machine learning. CSCI patients were randomly assigned to the training set (n = 203) and internal validation set (n = 87). A separate cohort comprising 245 CSCI patients were used for external validation. Independent predictors for POI were identified using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. A nomogram and an online calculator were developed and validated, both internally and externally. RESULTS Two inflammation-related endotypes were identified: high inflammation endotype (endotype C1) and low inflammation endotype (endotype C2). Eight predictors for POI were identified (including age, operation duration, number of surgical segments, time between injury and surgery, preoperative steroid pulse, American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) grade, smoking history, and inflammation-related endotype). A nomogram integrating the risk factors showed excellent discrimination in the training set (AUC, 0.976; 95% CI 0.956-0.996), internal validation set (AUC, 0.993; 95% CI 0.981-1.000), and external validation set (AUC, 0.799; 95%CI 0.744-0.854). Calibration curves demonstrated excellent fit, and decision curves highlighted its favorable clinical value. An online calculator (https://tjspine.shinyapps.io/dynnomapp/) was constructed to improve the convenience and efficiency of our prediction model. CONCLUSIONS We identified inflammation-related endotype and constructed a web-based calculator for predicting POI in patients with CSCI, exhibiting excellent clinical utility.

title: Adaptive Ai Defenses: Bridging Machine Learning and Cybersecurity for Next-Generation Threats
authors: Md Ismail Jobiullah
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Applications in Engineering
abstract: The various changes in cyber threats have made the old security systems to be more ineffective in reducing advanced attacks. Since the adversaries adapt, evade, and employ artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to establish adaptive and evasive methods, intelligent self-achieving defense is urgent. This article discusses the incorporation of AI adaptation frameworks into cybersecurity systems to battle the future-generation threats. Exploiting a comprehensive overview of existing ML research and practical deployments, the paper points to the superiority of reinforcement learning, adversarial ML, federated learning, and deep neural networks in building resilience against zero-day attacks, malware, phishing, and advanced persistent threats. An adaptation of this conceptual framework to the domain of adaptive AI defenses is advanced, with modeling of how continual model learning may enable the defender to close the gap between static defensive strategies and changing threats. In evidence-based case performance comparisons, adaptive AI-based systems can do better job in detecting with high accuracies, low false positives and scalability compared to conventional technologies. Concerns about adversarial manipulation, ethical issues, and computational requirements, as well as the provision of future paths, which consist of explainable AI, Policies, and quantum-computing based AI integration are other issues that are discussed in the discussion. This paper can therefore confidently draw adaptive AI defenses as one of the fundamental capabilities of safeguarding online infrastructures in view of the ever-evolving cybersecurity environment. DOI: https://doi.org/10.17762/ijisae.v12i23s.7826

title: ADBA:Approximation Decision Boundary Approach for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
authors: Feiyang Wang; Xingquan Zuo; Hai Huang; Gang Chen
abstract: Many machine learning models are susceptible to adversarial attacks, with decision-based black-box attacks representing the most critical threat in real-world applications. These attacks are extremely stealthy, generating adversarial examples using hard labels obtained from the target machine learning model. This is typically realized by optimizing perturbation directions, guided by decision boundaries identified through query-intensive exact search, significantly limiting the attack success rate. This paper introduces a novel approach using the Approximation Decision Boundary (ADB) to efficiently and accurately compare perturbation directions without precisely determining decision boundaries. The effectiveness of our ADB approach (ADBA) hinges on promptly identifying suitable ADB, ensuring reliable differentiation of all perturbation directions. For this purpose, we analyze the probability distribution of decision boundaries, confirming that using the distribution's median value as ADB can effectively distinguish different perturbation directions, giving rise to the development of the ADBA-md algorithm. ADBA-md only requires four queries on average to differentiate any pair of perturbation directions, which is highly query-efficient. Extensive experiments on six well-known image classifiers clearly demonstrate the superiority of ADBA and ADBA-md over multiple state-of-the-art black-box attacks. The source code is available at https://github.com/BUPTAIOC/ADBA.

title: AFF_CGE: Combined Attention-Aware Feature Fusion and Communication Graph Embedding Learning for Detecting Encrypted Malicious Traffic
authors: Junhao Liu; Guolin Shao; Hong Rao; Xiangjun Li; Xuan Huang
abstract: While encryption enhances data security, it also presents significant challenges for network traffic analysis, especially in detecting malicious activities. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces combined Attention-aware Feature Fusion and Communication Graph Embedding Learning (AFF_CGE), an advanced representation learning framework designed for detecting encrypted malicious traffic. By leveraging an attention mechanism and graph neural networks, AFF_CGE extracts rich semantic information from encrypted traffic and captures complex relations between communicating nodes. Experimental results reveal that AFF_CGE substantially outperforms traditional methods, improving F1-scores by 5.3% through 22.8%. The framework achieves F1-scores ranging from 0.903 to 0.929 across various classifiers, exceeding the performance of state-of-the-art techniques. These results underscore the effectiveness and robustness of AFF_CGE in detecting encrypted malicious traffic, demonstrating its superior performance.

title: AISec '24: 17th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security
authors: M. Pintor; Matthew Jagielski; Xinyun Chen
venue: Conference on Computer and Communications Security
abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) has been the center of the most outstanding advancements in the last years. The ability to analyze considerable streams of data in real time makes these technologies the most promising tool in many domains, including cybersecurity. As an outstanding example, ML can be used for identifying malware because of its ability to detect patterns otherwise difficult to see for humans and hard-coded rules. However, the use of AI and ML in security-relevant domains raised rightful concerns about their trustworthiness and robustness, espe- cially in front of adaptive attackers. Additionally, privacy threats are now emerging as a crucial aspect and need proper testing and possibly mitigation to prevent data stealing and leakage of sensitive information. AISec provides a venue for presenting and discussing new developments in the intersection of security and privacy with AI and ML. The AISec'24 workshop proceedings are available at: https://dl.acm.org/doi/proceedings/10.1145/3658644.3691545.
